Dicit autem Chrysostomus, quod audivit angelos, Gloria in excelsis Deo cantantes; angelum quoque evangelizantem pastoribus, Quia natus est vobis hodie Salvator. Vidit et Magos venientes, et puerum adorantes; verba etiam Simeonis et Annæ audivit, testimoniumque Joannis. Ex quibus conjiciebat Jesum esse Christum: præsertim quia ex vaticinio Danielis de numero hebdomadarum, cognovit tempus adventus Christi impletum. Ex prophetiis insuper Isaiæ et Jeremiæ: quorum unus ait, Vocabitur nomen ejus, Admirabilis, Consiliarius, Deus, Fortis, etc.; alius vero, Hoc est nomen quod vocabunt eum, Dominus justus noster (loco cujus in Hebræo habetur nomen Domini τετραγράμματον, quod soli vero convenit Deo): ex his, inquam, et aliis Prophetarum scripturis, sciebat quod Christus esset Deus et homo in una hypostasi seu persona. Ex quibus omnibus simul pensatis, vehementer opinatus est, quod Jesus esset Christus mundi Salvator. Sed ex alia parte, videns eum inter populares baptizatum, et fame confectum, dubitavit quomodo talis posset esse Deus et homo, seu Christus. Hinc ergo dixit ad eum:
paras.en: [[4:3|And the tempter coming said to him|Et accedens tentator, dixit ei]]. This tempter and demon is said to have been Lucifer, which the Master of the Sentences seems to hold; Hilary also testifies that he was the prince of the demons. He came to Christ in a visible and human form, and perhaps in the form of a religious man, so that, clothed in a feigned holiness, he might the sooner deceive. Now to tempt, taken in its proper sense, is to seek to learn by trial about something unknown or doubtful [Latin tentare means both “to tempt” and “to test, make trial of”]. The demon, then, was in doubt about Jesus of Nazareth, whether He was the Christ, and therefore he wished to be made certain of it; for he had reasons on either side that he could in some way not resolve. Chrysostom says that he heard the angels singing [[Luke 2:14|Glory to God in the highest|Gloria in excelsis Deo]], and the angel bringing the good news to the shepherds, [[Luke 2:11|For, this day is born to you a Saviour|Quia natus est vobis hodie Salvator]]. He saw too the Magi coming and adoring the Child; he heard also the words of Simeon and Anna, and the testimony of John. From these he conjectured that Jesus was the Christ: above all because from the prophecy of Daniel concerning the number of the weeks he knew that the time of the coming of Christ was fulfilled. And furthermore from the prophecies of Isaias and Jeremias, one of whom says, [[Is 9:6|his name shall be called Wonderful, Counsellor, God the Mighty|Vocabitur nomen ejus, Admirabilis, Consiliarius, Deus, Fortis]], etc., and the other, [[Jer 23:6|this is the name that they shall call him: The Lord our just one|Hoc est nomen quod vocabunt eum, Dominus justus noster]] (in place of which the Hebrew has the name of the Lord of four letters [the tetragrammaton, the divine name YHWH], which belongs to the true God alone): from these, I say, and from other writings of the Prophets, he knew that the Christ would be God and man in one hypostasis or person. Weighing all these things together, he was strongly of the opinion that Jesus was the Christ, the Saviour of the world. But on the other side, seeing Him baptized among the common people and worn with hunger, he doubted how such a one could be God and man, that is, the Christ. Hence, then, he said to Him:

paras.t: Si Filius Dei unigenitus, de quo locuti sunt Prophetæ, es, dic, id est, propria auctoritate jube, et dicendo effice, ut lapides isti, qui coram te jacent, panes fiant. Cogitavit autem diabolus versipellis: Si sine meo subsidio poterit propria potestate subito rerum naturas mutare, sciam quod sit universorum Creator, de quo legitur, Ipse dixit, et facta sunt; si autem non poterit, scio quod homo purus consistat. Tentavit autem de lapidum mutatione in panes, eo quod esset fame laborans, et per consequens magis inclinatus ad tale miraculum. Sed non est sapientia, nec est scientia, neque consilium contra Dominum. Sapientia enim in omnibus sapienter agit.
paras.en: [[4:3|If thou be the Son of God|Si Filius Dei unigenitus, de quo locuti sunt Prophetæ, es]] — the only-begotten, of whom the Prophets have spoken — [[4:3|command|dic]], that is, order it by thy own authority, and by speaking bring it about, [[4:3|that these stones|ut lapides isti]], which lie before thee, [[4:3|be made bread|panes fiant]]. For the wily devil thought: If without my help He can by His own power suddenly change the natures of things, I shall know that He is the Creator of all things, of whom we read, [[Ps 32:9|he spoke and they were made|Ipse dixit, et facta sunt]]; but if He cannot, I know that He is a mere man. He tempted Him with the changing of stones into bread because He was suffering from hunger, and was therefore the more inclined to such a miracle. But [[Prov 21:30|there is no wisdom|non est sapientia]], nor knowledge [Denis reads scientia, “knowledge”, where the Vulgate has prudentia, “prudence”], nor [[Prov 21:30|counsel against the Lord|consilium contra Dominum]]. For Wisdom acts wisely in all things.

paras.t: Quid ergo respondit Fons sapientiæ, Verbum Dei in excelsis, sequitur: Qui respondens, dicit ei: Scriptum est: Non in solo pane, id est corporeo cibo, vivit homo, secundum utramque partem suam, videlicet corpus et animam, sed in omni verbo sacræ Scripturæ, quod procedit de ore Dei, id est, ab intellectu divino inspiratur, et per os angelorum revelatur hominibus sanctis. Quemadmodum enim corpus sustentatur et conservatur in vita naturæ per panem materialem, sic anima conservatur ac roboratur in vita gratiæ per verbum Dei seu sacram Scripturam, quemadmodum ait Salvator: Qui audit verbum meum, et credit ei qui misit me, habet vitam æternam; et alibi, Beati qui audiunt verbum Dei, et custodiunt illud. Itaque verbum Dei intellectum illuminat, ad fidem inducit, opera dirigit, errores excludit: propter quod ait Psalmista, Lucerna pedibus meis verbum tuum, et lumen semitis meis. Spem roborat, juxta illud: Memor esto verbi tui servo tuo, in quo mihi spem dedisti. Caritatem accendit, juxta illud: Ignitum eloquium tuum vehementer. Animam consolatur, a voluptate avertit, timorem inducit: et breviter, sicut ait Apostolus, Omnis Scriptura divinitus inspirata, utilis est ad docendum, ad arguendum, ad erudiendum in justitia, ut perfectus sit homo ad omne opus bonum. Quemadmodum ergo merito desperatur vita naturalis ejus qui corporalem cibum non sumit, vel sumptum non retinet; sic rationabiliter desperatur spiritualis vita illius qui verbum Dei non audit atque custodit. Qui enim ex Deo est, verba Dei audit. Ait autem Ambrosius: Quum diabolus sic exploret ut tentet, et sic tentet ut exploret; Christus eum sic fallit ut vincat, et sic vincit ut fallat.
paras.en: What, then, did [[Ecclus 1:5|the fountain of wisdom|Fons sapientiæ]], [[Ecclus 1:5|the word of God on high|Verbum Dei in excelsis]], answer? There follows: [[4:4|Who answered and said|Qui respondens, dicit ei]]: [[4:4|It is written, Not in bread alone|Scriptum est: Non in solo pane]], that is, in bodily food, [[4:4|doth man live|vivit homo]], in both his parts, namely body and soul, [[4:4|but in every word|sed in omni verbo]] of Holy Scripture [[4:4|that proceedeth from the mouth of God|quod procedit de ore Dei]], that is, which is inspired by the divine understanding and revealed to holy men through the mouth of angels. For as the body is sustained and kept in the life of nature by material bread, so the soul is kept and strengthened in the life of grace by the word of God, that is, by Holy Scripture; as the Saviour says: [[John 5:24|he who heareth my word and believeth him that sent me hath life everlasting|Qui audit verbum meum, et credit ei qui misit me, habet vitam æternam]]; and elsewhere, [[Luke 11:28|blessed are they who hear the word of God and keep it|Beati qui audiunt verbum Dei, et custodiunt illud]]. And so the word of God enlightens the understanding, leads to faith, directs our works, shuts out errors; for which reason the Psalmist says: [[Ps 118:105|Thy word is a lamp to my feet, and a light to my paths|Lucerna pedibus meis verbum tuum, et lumen semitis meis]]. It strengthens hope, according to the words: [[Ps 118:49|Be thou mindful of thy word to thy servant, in which thou hast given me hope|Memor esto verbi tui servo tuo, in quo mihi spem dedisti]]. It kindles charity, according to the words: [[Ps 118:140|Thy word is exceedingly refined|Ignitum eloquium tuum vehementer]] [literally “Thy word is exceedingly fiery”; hence “kindles”]. It consoles the soul, turns it from pleasure, instils fear; and in short, as the Apostle says, [[2 Tim 3:16|All scripture, inspired of God, is profitable to teach, to reprove|Omnis Scriptura divinitus inspirata, utilis est ad docendum, ad arguendum]], [[2 Tim 3:16|to instruct in justice|ad erudiendum in justitia]], that man [[2 Tim 3:17|may be perfect|ut perfectus sit homo]] [[2 Tim 3:17|to every good work|ad omne opus bonum]]. As, therefore, the natural life of one who takes no bodily food, or does not keep down what he takes, is rightly despaired of, so the spiritual life of one who does not hear and keep the word of God is reasonably despaired of. For [[John 8:47|he that is of God heareth the words of God|Qui enim ex Deo est, verba Dei audit]]. And Ambrose says: Since the devil so explores as to tempt, and so tempts as to explore, Christ so deceives him as to conquer, and so conquers as to deceive.

paras.t: Advertendum autem tres esse species tentationis, ad quas aliæ reducuntur, videlicet gulæ, avaritiæ et superbiæ, prout Joannes asserit: Omne quod est in mundo, aut est concupiscentia carnis, aut concupiscentia oculorum, aut superbia vitæ. Istæ sunt arma diaboli contra famulos Dei. Quoniam ergo in prima tentatione, quæ fuit de gula, superatum se conspicit, aggreditur Christum per aliam tentationem, quæ est de superbia, vanaque gloria. Noverat quippe hostis versutus, viros perfectos, qui gulam facile vincunt, sæpe tangi motu superbiæ.
paras.en: Note that there are three kinds of temptation, to which the others are reduced, namely of gluttony, of avarice, and of pride; as John declares: [[1 John 2:16|all that is in the world|Omne quod est in mundo]] is either [[1 John 2:16|the concupiscence of the flesh|concupiscentia carnis]], or [[1 John 2:16|the concupiscence of the eyes|concupiscentia oculorum]], or [[1 John 2:16|the pride of life|superbia vitæ]]. These are the weapons of the devil against the servants of God. Since, then, he sees himself overcome in the first temptation, which was of gluttony, he attacks Christ with another temptation, which is of pride and vainglory. For the cunning enemy knew that perfect men, who easily overcome gluttony, are often touched by a motion of pride.

paras.t: Tunc assumpsit eum diabolus. Quomodo autem eum assumpserit, Scriptura non exprimit. Quidam vero affirmant, quod portavit eum in brachiis, vel humeris suis, tanquam fatigatum et debilem ex longo jejunio, et magnitudine famis, quasi compatiens ei: cui et Christus acquievit, ut falleret deceptorem. Aliqui dicunt, quod portavit eum volando per aerem: unde Lyra dicit, quod intentio dæmonis Christum portantis erat, ut Christus a populo volare videretur, atque ex hoc inaniter gloriaretur. Alii dicunt, quod duxit eum quasi manu ad manum per terram: quod magis consonare videtur ei quod in Luca habetur, Tunc duxit eum diabolus in Jerusalem. Aliquo ergo horum modorum assumpsit eum diabolus, non violenter, sed quasi ex prævia admonitione, ut iret ad homines causa vescendi, seu prædicandi, vel ob aliquid tale quod bonum videbatur. In sanctam civitatem, id est Jerusalem, in qua Sanctus Sanctorum sanguinem fudit, et primitiva Ecclesia Spiritum Sanctum recepit, atque evangelicam legem prædicare exorsa est. Et statuit, id est posuit, eum supra pinnaculum templi, id est deambulatorium seu tectum, quod fuerat planum, ubi sacerdotes sedebant quum populo prædicabant. Posuit autem eum illic præsente populo, ut Christus alliceretur ad laudem humanam, putans Christum videri ab omnibus. Sed ipse se invisibilem reddidit: in tantum enim fuit corpus ejus subjectum rationi ac Deo, quod ad imperium Dei ac propriæ rationis immutavit vel non immutavit visum aliorum, sicut et corpora glorificata.
paras.en: [[4:5|Then the devil took him up|Tunc assumpsit eum diabolus]]. How he took Him up, Scripture does not express. Some affirm that he carried Him in his arms or on his shoulders, as one wearied and weak from the long fast and the greatness of His hunger, as though pitying Him; and Christ consented to this, so as to deceive the deceiver. Others say that he carried Him flying through the air: hence Lyra says that the intention of the demon carrying Christ was that Christ should be seen flying by the people, and so be vainly puffed up by it. Others say that he led Him, as it were hand in hand, over the ground; and this seems to agree better with what is found in Luke: Then the devil [[Luke 4:9|brought him to Jerusalem|Tunc duxit eum diabolus in Jerusalem]]. In some one of these ways, then, the devil took Him up, not by force, but as it were by a prior suggestion that He should go among men for the sake of eating, or of preaching, or for some such thing that seemed good. [[4:5|into the holy city|In sanctam civitatem]], that is, Jerusalem, in which the Holy of Holies shed His blood, and the primitive Church received the Holy Ghost and began to preach the law of the Gospel; [[4:5|and set him|Et statuit]], that is, placed Him, [[4:5|upon the pinnacle of the temple|supra pinnaculum templi]], that is, the walk or roof, which was flat, where the priests sat when they preached to the people. He placed Him there in the presence of the people so that Christ might be enticed to human praise, supposing that Christ was seen by all. But He made Himself invisible; for His body was so far subject to reason and to God that, at the command of God and of His own reason, it affected or did not affect the sight of others, as glorified bodies also do.

paras.t: Et dixit ei: Si Filius Dei, Patri æqualis, es, mitte te deorsum in conspectu adstantium, ut videntes te sine casu volare, vel sine læsione cadere, mirentur et laudent te. Et ne timeas de periculo, scriptum est enim in Psalmo: Quoniam angelis suis mandavit, id est, præcepit Deus Pater, de te, id quod in psalmo illo subjungitur: Ut custodiant te in omnibus viis tuis; non autem in vanis præcipitiis: ideo dæmon subticuit hoc, ne sua fraudulentia notaretur a Jesu, quem scivit esse astutum ac providum. Et in manibus, id est sua virtute et operatione, tollent, id est portabunt te, quum fuerit opportunum, ne forte offendas ad lapidem pedem tuum, id est ne aliquid tibi in via obsistat aut lædat. Secundum Hieronymum, Bedam, et alios, psalmus iste non est ad litteram scriptus de Christo, sed de quocumque homine virtuoso et viatore, angelorum custodia indigente, qua Christus non eguit. In quo patet dolus diaboli, Scripturam mendaciter, et tamen verisimiliter seu multum apparenter applicantis.
paras.en: [[4:6|And said to him: If thou be the Son of God|Et dixit ei: Si Filius Dei, Patri æqualis, es]], equal to the Father, [[4:6|cast thyself down|mitte te deorsum]] in the sight of the bystanders, so that, seeing thee fly without falling, or fall without hurt, they may wonder at thee and praise thee. And do not fear the danger, [[4:6|for it is written|scriptum est enim]] in the Psalm: [[4:6|That he hath given his angels charge|Quoniam angelis suis mandavit]], that is, God the Father has commanded, [[4:6|over thee|de te]] that which is added in that psalm: [[Ps 90:11|to keep thee in all thy ways|Ut custodiant te in omnibus viis tuis]], but not in vain leaps from a height; and therefore the demon passed this over in silence, lest his deceit should be noticed by Jesus, whom he knew to be shrewd and far-seeing. [[4:6|and in their hands|Et in manibus]], that is, by their power and working, [[4:6|shall they bear thee up|tollent]], that is, carry thee, when it shall be fitting, [[4:6|lest perhaps thou dash thy foot against a stone|ne forte offendas ad lapidem pedem tuum]], that is, lest anything stand in thy way or harm thee. According to Jerome, Bede and others, that psalm is not written literally of Christ, but of any virtuous man who is a wayfarer and needs the guardianship of angels, which Christ did not need. In this the guile of the devil is plain, applying Scripture falsely, and yet plausibly, with a great show of fitness.

paras.t: Ait illi Jesus rursum: Scriptum est: Non tentabis Dominum Deum tuum, id est, o homo, quicumque sis ille, non præsumas Deum tentare. Non autem dixit Christus hæc verba, vocando se Deum diaboli, cujus utique Deus fuit; sed ut per veram allegationem Scripturæ impio prævaleret, ita quod nec ejus divinitas dæmoni patuit, nec aliquid certum de ejus conditione atque persona cognovit, an scilicet esset purus homo. Porro Deum tentare, est sine necessitate de ejus providentia vel potestate experimentum accipere, omittendo videlicet quod in se est et secundum humanum modum sibi incumbit, atque divinæ potentiæ se indiscrete committendo: ut si quis fame laborans, possit mendicando panem acquirere, sed hoc omittens, committit se divinæ providentiæ, non intelligens quod hoc ex divina providentia omnia complectente sit, quod possit mendicando acquirere panem. Quoniam ergo a pinnaculo templi ad pavimentum paratus fuit descensus per gradus, si Christus se præcipitasset, Deum videretur tentasse.
paras.en: [[4:7|Jesus said to him|Ait illi Jesus]]: [[4:7|It is written again|rursum: Scriptum est]]: [[4:7|Thou shalt not tempt the Lord thy God|Non tentabis Dominum Deum tuum]], that is, O man, whoever thou art, do not presume to tempt God. Christ did not say these words calling Himself the devil’s God, though He was indeed his God; but in order to prevail over the wicked one by a true citing of Scripture, in such a way that neither was His divinity made plain to the demon, nor did he learn anything certain about His condition and person, namely whether He was a mere man. Now to tempt God is to put His providence or power to the test without necessity: that is, to leave undone what lies in oneself and falls to one in the human way, and to commit oneself indiscreetly to the divine power; as if someone suffering from hunger could get bread by begging, but, neglecting this, commits himself to divine providence, not understanding that it comes from the divine providence that embraces all things that he is able to get bread by begging. Since, then, a way down by steps had been provided from the pinnacle of the temple to the pavement, if Christ had thrown Himself down He would have seemed to tempt God.

paras.t: Consequenter describitur tentatio tertia, quæ fuit de ambitione et avaritia, utpote de concupiscentia oculorum. Iterum assumpsit eum diabolus, forte eo modo ut ante, in montem excelsum valde, ut locus esset occasio consentiendi tentationi, sciens ex mutatione locorum frequenter mutari affectum; et ostendit ei omnia regna mundi principalia. Ostendit autem ei non ignoranti. Sed quomodo potuit ei omnia regna, id est urbes, terras, provincias mundi, demonstrare, quum certum sit nullum montem esse tam altum, ut ab eo omnes provinciæ possint videri? Et licet satis altus consisteret, tamen propter localem distantiam, visum constituti in monte immutare nequaquam valerent. Respondendum, quod ostendit ei omnia regna mundi, non quia objecit ea oculis intuenda determinate et corporaliter, sed proxima regna ostendit ad oculum, quantum fieri potuit, versus quatuor plagas mundi; cetera vero dixit in tali, vel tali parte terræ situata: velut si aliquis exsistens in turri cum alio, dicat, Ecce ibi est Roma, ibi Leodium, ibi Colonia. Et gloriam eorum, id est, pompas, delicias atque divitias regnorum terrenorum exposuit Christo. Et dixit ei: Hæc omnia tibi dabo, si cadens, genua flectendo, vel in terram te prosternendo, adoraveris me adoratione latriæ. Hæc est antiqua et solita dæmonis pompa, ut Deo assimilari et a concreaturis adorari desideret.
paras.en: Next the third temptation is described, which was of ambition and avarice, that is, of the concupiscence of the eyes. [[4:8|Again the devil took him up|Iterum assumpsit eum diabolus]], perhaps in the same way as before, [[4:8|into a very high mountain|in montem excelsum valde]], so that the place might be an occasion of consenting to the temptation, knowing that with a change of place the affections often change; [[4:8|and shewed him all the kingdoms of the world|et ostendit ei omnia regna mundi]], the principal ones. He showed them, indeed, to One who was not ignorant of them. But how could he show Him all the kingdoms, that is, the cities, lands and provinces of the world, since it is certain that no mountain is so high that all the provinces can be seen from it? And even if one were high enough, still, because of the distance, they could not affect the sight of one standing on the mountain. The answer is that he showed Him all the kingdoms of the world, not by setting them distinctly and bodily before His eyes to be gazed at, but he showed the nearest kingdoms to the eye, as far as could be done, towards the four quarters of the world, and of the rest he said that they lay in such or such a part of the earth: as if someone standing in a tower with another were to say, Look, there is Rome, there Liège, there Cologne. [[4:8|and the glory of them|Et gloriam eorum]], that is, the pomps, delights and riches of the earthly kingdoms, he set forth to Christ. [[4:9|And said to him: All these will I give thee, if falling down|Et dixit ei: Hæc omnia tibi dabo, si cadens]], by bending the knee or prostrating thyself on the ground, [[4:9|thou wilt adore me|adoraveris me]] with the adoration of latria [that is, the worship due to God alone]. This is the ancient and accustomed pomp of the demon, that he desires to be made like God and to be adored by his fellow creatures.

paras.t: Tunc dicit ei Jesus: Vade, id est, recede a me, Satana, id est, adversarie veritatis. Vade, inquam, in ignem æternum, secundum Hieronymum. Verumtamen tempore passionis creditur redisse, et Christum per Judæos tentasse. Scriptum est enim: Dominum Deum tuum adorabis adoratione interiori et exteriori, et illi soli servies propter se atque finaliter. Vel loquitur de servitute latriæ, quæ Deo dumtaxat debetur. Soli ergo Deo serviendum est propter se: quia etsi aliis non solum superioribus, sed etiam æqualibus ac inferioribus serviendum sit, pro loco, causa et tempore (juxta illud Apostoli: Per caritatem servite in invicem; et Salvator in Evangelio, Qui major, inquit, est vestrum, sit vester minister), omnis tamen servitus ista ad Dei honorem referenda est, et propter ejus ordinationem ac voluntatem impendenda; neque alicui serviendum vel obediendum est in his quæ divinitus prohibentur, quemadmodum Petrus testatur: Quia obedire oportet Deo magis quam hominibus. Quum igitur homini ministramus, non tam homini quam Deo in homine ministremus, præsertim quum dicat Salvator: Quod uni ex minimis meis fecistis, mihi fecistis. Servitus autem duliæ, hominibus potest et debet impendi. Quum enim Deus sit summus in se, et maximus benefactor noster, atque altissimus princeps universorum, propria potestate potens salvare quoscumque voluerit; constat quod summa et singularis ei reverentia debeatur, videlicet cultus latriæ.
paras.en: [[4:10|Then Jesus saith to him: Begone|Tunc dicit ei Jesus: Vade]], that is, depart from me, [[4:10|Satan|Satana]], that is, adversary of the truth [the name Satan means “adversary”]. Begone, I say, into the everlasting fire, according to Jerome. Yet he is believed to have returned at the time of the Passion and to have tempted Christ through the Jews. [[4:10|for it is written: The Lord thy God shalt thou adore|Scriptum est enim: Dominum Deum tuum adorabis]] with inward and outward adoration, [[4:10|and him only shalt thou serve|et illi soli servies]] for His own sake and as the last end. Or He speaks of the service of latria, which is owed to God alone. God alone, then, is to be served for His own sake: for although others too are to be served — not only superiors, but equals and inferiors as well — according to place, cause and time (as in the words of the Apostle, [[Gal 5:13|by charity|Per caritatem]] [[Gal 5:13|serve one another|servite in invicem]]; and the Saviour in the Gospel: [[Matt 23:11|He that is the greatest among you|Qui major, inquit, est vestrum]], let him be [[Matt 23:11|your servant|vester minister]]), yet all such service is to be referred to the honour of God, and rendered because of His ordinance and will; nor is anyone to be served or obeyed in those things that are forbidden by God, as Peter testifies: [[Acts 5:29|We ought to obey God rather than men|Quia obedire oportet Deo magis quam hominibus]]. When, therefore, we minister to a man, let us minister not so much to the man as to God in the man; above all since the Saviour says: What you did to one of the least of mine, [[Matt 25:40|you did it to me|mihi fecistis]]. The service of dulia [that is, the honour and service that may rightly be paid to creatures], however, can and should be rendered to men. For since God is supreme in Himself, and our greatest benefactor, and the most high prince of all things, able by His own power to save whomever He will, it is clear that supreme and singular reverence is owed to Him, namely the worship of latria.

paras.t: Considerandum in Christi responsionibus, quomodo falsas de Scripturis a diabolo sumptas sagittas, veris Scripturarum clypeis rejiciat atque confringat.
paras.en: Consider in Christ’s answers how He drives back and breaks the false arrows the devil took from the Scriptures with the true shields of the Scriptures.

paras.t: Tunc reliquit eum in monte isto sublimi, diabolus, confusus et victus recedens, nec aliquid certum de Christi persona cognoscens. Et ecce angeli accesserunt motu repentino ad Jesum in monte, et ministrabant ei, non quasi inferiori aut indigenti, sed ut Domino, cum humilitate et reverentia, deponendo eum de cacumine montis ad terræ planitiem. Quia enim humanam assumpsit naturam, humano modo se habuit, conformando se fratribus, atque angelico famulatu utendo. Nec solum hac vice, sed etiam prius angeli ministrabant ei in eremo, juxta illud: Spiritus expulit eum in desertum; eratque cum bestiis, et angeli ministrabant ei. In quibus omnibus divinæ naturæ sublimitas, et item humanæ naturæ declivitas manifestantur in Christo.
paras.en: [[4:11|Then the devil left him|Tunc reliquit eum in monte isto sublimi, diabolus]] on that lofty mountain, withdrawing confounded and conquered, and knowing nothing certain about the person of Christ. [[4:11|and behold angels came|Et ecce angeli accesserunt]] with a sudden movement to Jesus on the mountain, [[4:11|and ministered to him|et ministrabant ei]], not as to an inferior or one in need, but as to their Lord, with humility and reverence, setting Him down from the summit of the mountain to the level ground. For because He had taken human nature, He bore Himself in a human way, making Himself like His brethren and making use of the service of angels. And not only on this occasion, but earlier too the angels ministered to Him in the wilderness, according to the words: [[Mark 1:12|the Spirit drove him out into the desert|Spiritus expulit eum in desertum]]; [[Mark 1:13|And he was with beasts: and the angels ministered to him|eratque cum bestiis, et angeli ministrabant ei]]. In all these things the loftiness of the divine nature and likewise the lowliness of the human nature are made manifest in Christ.

paras.t: Circa præinducta primo inquiritur, cur Lucas tentationem factam super pinnaculum templi ponit tertiam, quam Matthæus ponit secundam. Ad hoc quidam dixerunt, Lucam describere tentationes has Christi secundum ordinem factas, ita quod Christus secundo tentatus est in monte excelso, quem dicunt fuisse in eodem deserto in quo facta est prima tentatio: sicque in montem, quasi in locum propinquiorem, duxit eum diabolus statim post primam tentationem. Matthæum vero dicunt descripsisse tentationes Christi, non secundum ordinem rei gestæ, sed juxta quamdam correspondentiam ad tentationem primorum parentum, qui primo tentati fuerunt de gula, secundo de superbia, tertio de avaritia. Hæc autem responsio non videtur conveniens. Evangelista namque Matthæus apertissime docet, quod diabolus Christum reliquerit quasi confusus et victus, audita responsione Christi qua dæmonem de avaritia tentantem, et idololatriam quodammodo suggerentem, dire objurgans dicebat: Vade, Satana. Ergo tentatio ista ultimo facta est. Denique Lucas descripta tentatione in pinnaculo facta, quam tertiam ponit, non dicit, quod tunc reliquit eum diabolus; sed, Omni (inquit) consummata tentatione, recessit ab eo usque ad tempus. Non ergo recessit ante eam quæ in monte completa est, post quam dicit eum recessisse Matthæus. Hæc ergo ultima fuit. Hoc quoque patet per hoc quod tentatio dæmonis gradatim processit ad deteriora: tertia autem, in qua se adorari suggessit, pessima fuit. Verumtamen Augustinus asserit nos ignorare, quæ duarum ultimarum tentationum præcesserit; et dicit non referre quæ ante aliam recitetur, quia Scriptura non semper recitat gesta ordine illo quo facta sunt.
paras.en: Concerning what has been set out, it is asked first why Luke puts third the temptation that took place on the pinnacle of the temple, which Matthew puts second. To this some have said that Luke describes these temptations of Christ in the order in which they happened, so that Christ was tempted second on the high mountain, which they say was in the same desert in which the first temptation took place; and so the devil led Him to the mountain, as to the nearer place, immediately after the first temptation. Matthew, they say, described the temptations of Christ not in the order of events, but according to a certain correspondence with the temptation of our first parents, who were tempted first of gluttony, secondly of pride, thirdly of avarice. But this answer does not seem fitting. For Matthew the Evangelist teaches most plainly that the devil left Christ, as one confounded and conquered, on hearing the answer of Christ, in which, sternly rebuking the demon who was tempting Him to avarice and in a manner suggesting idolatry, He said: [[4:10|Begone, Satan|Vade, Satana]]. That temptation, therefore, came last. Moreover Luke, having described the temptation on the pinnacle, which he puts third, does not say that the devil then left Him, but, [[Luke 4:13|all the temptation being ended|Omni (inquit) consummata tentatione]], he says, he [[Luke 4:13|departed from him for a time|recessit ab eo usque ad tempus]]. He did not depart, then, before the temptation that was completed on the mountain, after which Matthew says that he departed. That one, therefore, was the last. This is also plain from the fact that the demon’s temptation went on by degrees to worse things; and the third, in which he suggested that he be adored, was the worst. Augustine, however, asserts that we do not know which of the last two temptations came first, and says that it does not matter which is told before the other, since Scripture does not always tell events in the order in which they happened.

paras.t: Insuper quæritur, an tentator duxit Christum invitum, vel quasi spontaneum, hoc est, an putavit quod Christus secum tendebat libenter, vel magis coacte. Respondendum secundum Hieronymum et Chrysostomum, quod dæmon voluntatem Christi putavit infirmitatem ac necessitatem, putans se eum compellere ad proficiscendum secum. Alii vero satis probabiliter dicunt, quod dæmon in specie viri religiosi apparens, et Christum decipere cupiens, blandiebatur ei, et suam malitiam occultabat, ne sciretur esse diabolus: sicque Christum quasi spontaneum secum assumpsit. Ex quo sequi videtur, quod non volavit secum per aera. Sic enim patuisset eum non hominem esse. Nihilo minus in tertia tentatione, in qua manifestum crimen suasit, ostendit se non esse talem qualis apparuit. Cernens quippe se per simulationem sanctitatis et allegationem Scripturarum nihil proficere, manifestam iniquitatem proposuit, ad quam ut induceret, magnum obtulit præmium, utpote omnia regna mundi. Qui quia diabolus dicit se posse dare, Manichæi opinabantur omnia ista terrena a diabolo esse creata, ejusque imperio ad nutum subjecta. Sed hoc dictum stultum ac debile est. Quum enim diabolus sit mendax et arrogans, non vere sed præsumptuose asseruit se regna omnia posse dare alicui: nisi intelligatur quod permissione divina frequenter diabolus cooperatur aliquibus ad obtinenda dominia mundi. Quod vero non sit sic intelligendum, quasi propria potestate et jure creationis valeat ea dare alicui, evidentissime constat per illud quod apud Lucam habetur, dicente ad Christum diabolo: Tibi dabo potestatem hanc universam et gloriam illorum, quoniam mihi tradita sunt.
paras.en: It is asked further whether the tempter led Christ against His will or as one going of His own accord; that is, whether he thought that Christ went with him willingly, or rather under constraint. The answer, according to Jerome and Chrysostom, is that the demon took Christ’s will for weakness and necessity, thinking that he was compelling Him to go with him. Others, however, say quite probably that the demon, appearing in the guise of a religious man and wishing to deceive Christ, flattered Him and hid his malice, lest he should be known to be the devil; and so he took Christ with him as one going of His own accord. From this it seems to follow that he did not fly with Him through the air, for so it would have been plain that he was not a man. Nevertheless, in the third temptation, in which he urged an open crime, he showed that he was not such as he had appeared. For seeing that he gained nothing by feigning holiness and by citing the Scriptures, he proposed open iniquity, and to lead Him to it he offered a great reward, namely all the kingdoms of the world. Because the devil says he can give these, the Manichees held that all these earthly things were created by the devil and are subject to his rule at his nod. But this saying is foolish and weak. For since the devil is a liar and arrogant, he asserted not truly but presumptuously that he could give all the kingdoms to anyone; unless it be understood that by divine permission the devil often works together with some men to gain the lordships of the world. That it is not to be understood as though by his own power and by right of creation he could give them to anyone is most evidently clear from what is found in Luke, where the devil says to Christ: [[Luke 4:6|To thee will I give all this power and the glory of them. For to me they are delivered|Tibi dabo potestatem hanc universam et gloriam illorum, quoniam mihi tradita sunt]].

paras.t: Postremo, per hoc quod Christus duas primas tentationes ad suam injuriam pertinentes, cum mansuetudine pertulit, solum ad verba Satanæ congruenter respondens; tertiam vero tentationem cum exprobratione quasi exasperatus rejecit, dicens tentanti, Vade, Satana: per hoc, inquam, secundum Chrysostomum, edocemur, nostras injurias magnanimiter sustinere, Dei autem injurias et contemptum, nec usque ad auditum sufferre: quoniam in propriis injuriis patientem esse laudabile est, injurias autem Dei dissimulare nimis est impium.
paras.en: Lastly, in that Christ bore with meekness the first two temptations, which touched His own injury, only answering the words of Satan fittingly, but rejected the third temptation with reproach, as though provoked, saying to the tempter, [[4:10|Begone, Satan|Vade, Satana]]: by this, I say, according to Chrysostom, we are taught to bear our own injuries with greatness of soul, but not to suffer injuries and contempt against God even so far as to hear them; for to be patient under one’s own injuries is praiseworthy, but to pass over injuries done to God is exceedingly impious.

paras.t: Insuper, per hoc quod Christum post Baptismum atque Jejunium tentator aggressus est, insinuatur tunc quemlibet nostrum fortius a diabolo impugnari, vel etiam a proximis infestari, quum vehementiori affectu applicamus cor nostrum puritati internæ ac veræ devotioni. Tunc enim fremit et furit impiissimus hostis, incitatque frequenter proximos nostros adversum nos. Nos vero invictissimo animo insistamus custodiæ cordis, tanto ardentius quanto sentimus nos durius impeti ac tentari, dicentes cum Propheta: Persequar inimicos meos, et comprehendam illos; et non convertar donec deficiant. Et ita vere in nobis implebitur quod dicit Apostolus: Deus conteret Satanam sub pedibus vestris velociter.
paras.en: Moreover, in that the tempter attacked Christ after His Baptism and fast, it is suggested that each of us is assailed more strongly by the devil, or even harassed by our neighbours, at the time when we apply our heart with more ardent affection to inward purity and true devotion. For then the most wicked enemy rages and storms, and often stirs up our neighbours against us. But let us, with an unconquerable spirit, hold fast to the guarding of the heart, the more ardently the harder we feel ourselves assailed and tempted, saying with the Prophet: [[Ps 17:38|I will pursue after my enemies, and overtake them: and I will not turn again till they are consumed|Persequar inimicos meos, et comprehendam illos; et non convertar donec deficiant]]. And so there will truly be fulfilled in us what the Apostle says: God will [[Rom 16:20|crush Satan under your feet speedily|conteret Satanam sub pedibus vestris velociter]].

paras.t: Rursus, per hoc quod Christus dejecit diabolum allegando Scripturas, instruimur tentationibus obviandum esse Scripturis divinis, unicuique tentationi objiciendo Scripturam contra tale vel tale peccatum de quo tentamur: ut si de elatione tentemur, cogitemus quod scriptum est, Odibilis coram Deo et hominibus est superbia; et illud, Deus superbis resistit, humilibus autem dat gratiam. Si de invidia, cogitemus illud B. Joannis: Omnis qui odit fratrem suum, homicida est.
paras.en: Again, in that Christ cast down the devil by citing the Scriptures, we are taught that temptations are to be met with the divine Scriptures, setting against each temptation the Scripture that speaks against the particular sin with which we are tempted: so that if we are tempted to pride, we should think of what is written, [[Ecclus 10:7|Pride is hateful before God and men|Odibilis coram Deo et hominibus est superbia]], and of this: [[Jas 4:6|God resisteth the proud and giveth grace to the humble|Deus superbis resistit, humilibus autem dat gratiam]]. If to envy, let us think of the words of blessed John: [[1 John 3:15|Whosoever hateth his brother is a murderer|Omnis qui odit fratrem suum, homicida est]].

paras.t: Porro modus qui dictus est, quomodo scilicet diabolus ostendit Christo omnia regna mundi, videtur quibusdam superficialis. Unde quasi subtilius loqui volentes, dicunt, quod quum intelligentia sit plena formis, diabolus, qui omnium regnorum species in se continebat, potuit eas præsentare intellectui animæ Christi, et ita omnia regna sibi ostendere; vel etiam depingendo ea in terra, sicut fit in mappa mundi; vel exponendo ei dispositionem regnorum. Quamvis autem hujusmodi ostensiones fieri potuissent, tamen propter eas dæmon non indiguisset Christum in montem altum assumere, quia tam convenienter fieri possunt in valle sicut in monte. Ideo præinductus modus, qui etiam concordat Chrysostomo, rationabilior æstimatur.
paras.en: The way that has been described, however, namely how the devil showed Christ all the kingdoms of the world, seems superficial to some. Hence, wishing to speak as it were more subtly, they say that since an intelligence is full of forms [a scholastic axiom: an angelic intellect holds within itself the forms, or ideas, of things], the devil, who contained within himself the images of all kingdoms, could present them to the understanding of Christ’s soul, and so show Him all the kingdoms; or else by drawing them on the ground, as is done in a map of the world; or by explaining to Him the arrangement of the kingdoms. But although such showings could have been made, still the demon would not have needed to take Christ up into a high mountain for them, since they can be made as conveniently in a valley as on a mountain. Therefore the way set out before, which also agrees with Chrysostom, is judged the more reasonable.

4.title: Prosecutio expositionis hujus capituli quarti, ab eo loco quo dicitur: Quum autem audisset Jesus
4.title_en: Continuation of the exposition of this fourth chapter, from the place where it says: “And when Jesus had heard”

paras.t: Recitata Domini Salvatoris tentatione, prosequitur Evangelista ordinem et processum conversationis, instructionis et miraculorum ipsius. Porro, ut Beda testatur in prologo suo super Joannem, Matthæus, Lucas, Marcus referunt Christum post incarcerationem Joannis Baptistæ cœpisse miracula facere, id est, ea omittunt quæ ante incarcerationem hanc fiebant a Christo, videlicet mutationem aquæ in vinum, sanationem filii reguli, et cetera quæ Joannes in suis capitulis describit. Cœpit ergo Jesus prædicare, discipulos congregare, per Apostolos baptizare, et signa facere, ante incarcerationem Joannis; idcirco evangelista Joannes, qui ultimus evangelium scripsit, et aliorum trium evangelium legit, supplevit quod illi omiserunt. Verumtamen Christus non prædicavit tam aperte, nec miracula fecit tam copiose ante incarcerationem Joannis, ut postea. Propterea tres Evangelistæ satis putaverunt, si facta et documenta Christi post incarcerationem Joannis exhibita prosequerentur, quamvis unusquisque eorum multa omiserit: nam omnes tres suscitationem Lazari omiserunt. Unde non mirum, si multa quoque omiserunt minora.
paras.en: Having recounted the temptation of the Lord our Saviour, the Evangelist goes on with the order and course of His manner of life, His teaching and His miracles. Now, as Bede testifies in his prologue on John, Matthew, Luke and Mark relate that Christ began to work miracles after the imprisonment of John the Baptist; that is, they leave out the things that were done by Christ before this imprisonment, namely the changing of water into wine, the healing of the ruler’s son, and the other things that John describes in his chapters. For Jesus began to preach, to gather disciples, to baptize through the Apostles, and to work signs before John’s imprisonment; and therefore John the evangelist, who wrote his gospel last and had read the gospel of the other three, supplied what they had left out. Nevertheless, before John’s imprisonment Christ did not preach so openly, nor work miracles so abundantly, as afterwards. That is why the three Evangelists thought it enough to set down the deeds and teachings of Christ shown forth after John’s imprisonment, although each of them left out many things: for all three left out the raising of Lazarus. So it is no wonder if they also left out many lesser things.

paras.t: Exordium itaque sumens Matthæus ab operibus Christi quæ post Joannis incarcerationem contigerunt, subjecit: Quum autem audisset Jesus a discipulis Joannis vel propriis (quod tamen certissime præcognovit), videlicet quod Joannes Baptista traditus esset, a Deo permissive, in manum Herodis Antipæ, et ab Herode in manum servorum suorum, ut Joannem incarcerarent, eo quod illicitas nuptias Herodis ac Herodiadis increpasset; secessit in Galilæam, id est, a loco quo captus est Joannes se elongavit, cedens furori Herodis, ne occideretur ab eo, secundum Chrysostomum: non quod timuit mortem, sed ut opportuniore tempore pateretur, et item ut fugiendi daret exemplum quando non prodest comparere. Et relicta civitate Nazareth, in qua fuit conceptus et nutritus, venit et habitavit in civitate dicta Capharnaum maritima, id est supra mare Genesareth sita, in cujus littore sitæ erant Capharnaum, Tiberias, Bethsaida, Corozain, civitates pertinentes ad fines Zabulon ac Nephthali: ideo subditur, In finibus, id est sorte seu terminis, Zabulon ac Nephthali, scilicet duarum tribuum, ad quarum unam pertinebat Capharnaum. Unde Christus habitando in Capharnaum, habitavit in finibus Zabulon et Nephthali, id est inter fines et urbes Judæorum descendentium de tribu ac semine Zabulon et Nephthali.
paras.en: Taking his beginning, then, from the works of Christ that came about after John’s imprisonment, Matthew added: [[4:12|And when Jesus had heard|Quum autem audisset Jesus]], from John’s disciples or from His own (though He most certainly knew it beforehand), namely [[4:12|that John was delivered up|quod Joannes traditus esset]], by God’s permission, into the hand of Herod Antipas, and by Herod into the hand of his servants, that they might imprison John, because he had rebuked the unlawful marriage of Herod and Herodias, [[4:12|he retired into Galilee|secessit in Galilæam]]; that is, He went away from the place where John was taken, giving way to Herod’s fury lest He be killed by him, according to Chrysostom: not that He feared death, but that He might suffer at a more fitting time, and also that He might give an example of fleeing when it does no good to show oneself. [[4:13|And leaving the city Nazareth|Et relicta civitate Nazareth]], in which He was conceived and brought up, [[4:13|he came and dwelt in|venit et habitavit in]] the city called [[4:13|Capharnaum on the sea coast|Capharnaum maritima]], that is, lying on the sea of Genesareth, on whose shore lay Capharnaum, Tiberias, Bethsaida and Corozain, cities belonging to the borders of Zabulon and Nephthali. Therefore it is added: [[4:13|in the borders|In finibus]], that is, in the lot or territory, [[4:13|of Zabulon and of Nephthalim|Zabulon ac Nephthali]], that is, of two tribes, to one of which Capharnaum belonged. So Christ, by dwelling in Capharnaum, dwelt in the borders of Zabulon and Nephthali, that is, among the borders and cities of the Jews descended from the tribe and seed of Zabulon and Nephthali.

paras.t: Ut adimpleretur quod dictum est a Spiritu Sancto per Isaiam prophetam: Terra Zabulon, et terra Nephthali, quæ est via maris, id est, in qua est via communis, qua deferuntur merces a Jordane ad mare Mediterraneum, trans Jordanem, id est, per quam viam itur trans Jordanem, tendendo in ea usque Jordanem, Galilææ gentium, id est, juxta quam est Galilæa gentium, id est provincia illa quam in libris Regum legitur Salomon dedisse Hiram regi Tyri, cui dedit viginti oppida in Galilæa. Et quoniam Hiram fuit gentilis, illa pars Galilææ vocata est Galilæa gentium, quam ipse Hiram appellavit terram Chabul. Vel sic: Via maris trans Jordanem, id est via qua itur a mari prædicto ad Jordanem Galilææ gentium. Hæc igitur terra dicitur via, quoniam via publica erat in ea. Quid autem per terram Zabulon et terram Nephthali principaliter intelligatur, subjungit: Populus qui ambulabat in tenebris, id est habitatores harum terrarum, qui conversabantur in tenebris ignorantiæ, perfidiæ, et peccati, vidit lucem magnam, videlicet Christum, qui ait: Ego sum lux mundi.
paras.en: [[4:14|That it might be fulfilled which was said|Ut adimpleretur quod dictum est]] by the Holy Ghost [[4:14|by Isaias the prophet|per Isaiam prophetam]]: [[4:15|Land of Zabulon and land of Nephthalim|Terra Zabulon, et terra Nephthali]], which is [[4:15|the way of the sea|via maris]], that is, in which is the common road by which merchandise is carried from the Jordan to the Mediterranean Sea; [[4:15|beyond the Jordan|trans Jordanem]], that is, by which road one goes beyond the Jordan, travelling along it as far as the Jordan; [[4:15|Galilee of the Gentiles|Galilææ gentium]], that is, beside which lies Galilee of the Gentiles, namely that province which, as we read in the books of Kings, Solomon gave to Hiram king of Tyre, to whom he gave twenty towns in Galilee. And because Hiram was a gentile, that part of Galilee was called Galilee of the Gentiles, which Hiram himself called the land of Chabul. Or thus: [[4:15|the way of the sea beyond the Jordan|Via maris trans Jordanem]], that is, the road by which one goes from the sea just mentioned to the Jordan of Galilee of the Gentiles. This land, then, is called a way, because there was a public road in it. And what is chiefly meant by the land of Zabulon and the land of Nephthali, he adds: [[4:16|The people|Populus]] that walked [[4:16|in darkness|in tenebris]] [Denis reads qui ambulabat, “that walked”, as in Isaias 9:2, where the Vulgate of Matthew has qui sedebat, “that sat”.], that is, the inhabitants of these lands, who lived in the darkness of ignorance, of unbelief and of sin, [[4:16|hath seen great light|vidit lucem magnam]], namely Christ, who says: [[John 8:12|I am the light of the world|Ego sum lux mundi]].

paras.t: Allegatio Evangelistæ decurtata est, et dum brevitati studuit, obscuritatem induxit. Ad pleniorem ergo intelligentiam habendam, sciendum quod in Isaia sic dicitur: Primo tempore alleviata est terra Zabulon et terra Nephthali, et novissime aggravata est via maris trans Jordanem Galilææ gentium; populus qui ambulabat, etc., sicut nunc allegatur. Est itaque sensus: Primo tempore, id est in principio evangelicæ prædicationis factæ ab ipso Christo, alleviata est terra Zabulon et terra Nephthali, id est habitatores terrarum istarum, videlicet nati de Zabulon et Nephthali, qui pro majori parte translati et capti fuerunt diu ante Christi adventum: aliqui tamen remanserunt, de quibus nunc agitur. Hi ergo alleviati sunt, et animo relevati a jugo diaboli et servitute peccati. In his etenim locis cœpit Jesus prædicare et signa facere, credideruntque multi in eum. E novissimo, id est circa finem prædicationis Christi, aggravata est via maris: id est, populus iste in his terris habitans oneratus est vitiis, induratusque corde, revertens ad vomitum, et fidem doctrinamque Christi abjiciens. Unde infra Salvator exprobrat civitatibus istis, dicens: Væ tibi, Bethsaida; væ tibi, Corozain, etc. Populus iste qui ambulabat in tenebris vidit lucem magnam: nam oculis cordis viderunt et intellexerunt Christi doctrinam; sedentibus*, id est degentibus seu manentibus, in regione umbræ mortis, id est in terra plena peccatis: quæ sunt umbræ mortis, quoniam lucem gratiæ abscondunt, et morti æternæ proximum faciunt. Lux christianæ veritatis orta est eis.
paras.en: The Evangelist’s citation is cut short, and while he aimed at brevity he brought in obscurity. For a fuller understanding, then, it should be known that in Isaias it is said thus: [[Is 9:1|At the first time the land of Zabulon, and the land of Nephtali was lightly touched: and at the last the way of the sea beyond the Jordan of the Galilee of the Gentiles was heavily loaded|Primo tempore alleviata est terra Zabulon et terra Nephthali, et novissime aggravata est via maris trans Jordanem Galilææ gentium]] [the Latin alleviata est means “was lightened” or “relieved”, and Denis takes it in that sense below]; [[Is 9:2|the people that walked|populus qui ambulabat]], etc., as it is now cited. The sense, then, is this: [[Is 9:1|At the first time|Primo tempore]], that is, at the beginning of the gospel preaching done by Christ Himself, [[Is 9:1|the land of Zabulon, and the land of Nephtali was lightly touched|alleviata est terra Zabulon et terra Nephthali]], that is, the inhabitants of those lands, namely those born of Zabulon and Nephthali, who for the most part had been carried away captive long before Christ’s coming; some, however, remained, and it is of these that he now speaks. These, then, were lightened, and relieved in spirit from the yoke of the devil and the bondage of sin; for in these places Jesus began to preach and to work signs, and many believed in Him. [[Is 9:1|And at the last|E novissimo]], that is, about the end of Christ’s preaching, [[Is 9:1|the way of the sea|via maris]] [[Is 9:1|was heavily loaded|aggravata est]]: that is, this people dwelling in these lands was weighed down with vices and hardened in heart, returning to its vomit and casting off the faith and teaching of Christ. Hence below the Saviour reproaches these cities, saying: [[Matt 11:21|woe to thee, Bethsaida|Væ tibi, Bethsaida]]; [[Matt 11:21|woe|væ]] to [[Matt 11:21|thee, Corozain|tibi, Corozain]], etc. This [[Is 9:2|people that walked in darkness, have seen a great light|Populus iste qui ambulabat in tenebris vidit lucem magnam]]: for with the eyes of the heart they saw and understood the teaching of Christ; [[4:16|to them that sat|sedentibus]], that is, that lived or abode, [[4:16|in the region of the shadow of death|in regione umbræ mortis]], that is, in a land full of sins, which are the shadows of death, because they hide the light of grace and bring a man near to eternal death, [[4:16|light|Lux]] of Christian truth [[4:16|is sprung up|orta est eis]].

paras.t: Exinde, id est post traditionem Joannis et mansionem in Capharnaum, cœpit Jesus prædicare manifeste et quasi continuo: tamen et ante incepit; et dicere: Pœnitentiam agite, appropinquavit enim regnum cælorum. Tale fuit etiam exordium prædicationis Joannis: cujus prædicationem volens confirmare Salvator, et ostendere quod ipse sit de quo Joannes testatus est, simili modo exorsus est. Hæc autem verba supra exposita sunt.
paras.en: [[4:17|From that time|Exinde]], that is, after John was delivered up and after He took up His dwelling in Capharnaum, [[4:17|Jesus began to preach|cœpit Jesus prædicare]] openly and, as it were, without a break (though He had begun even before), [[4:17|and to say: Do penance, for the kingdom of heaven is at hand|et dicere: Pœnitentiam agite, appropinquavit enim regnum cælorum]]. Such too was the opening of John’s preaching; and the Saviour, wishing to confirm John’s preaching and to show that He Himself was the one to whom John had borne witness, began in the same way. These words have been explained above.

paras.t: Ambulans autem Jesus juxta mare Galilææ, quod alio nomine vocatur stagnum Genesareth: eratque lacus magnus, secundum Hieronymum; sed dicitur mare juxta consuetudinem idiomatis Hebræorum, qui quamlibet magnam congregationem aquarum nominant mare. Vidit duos fratres, videlicet Simonem, qui vocatur alio nomine Petrus, id est firmus, et Cephas, id est principalis: quæ duo nomina Christus sibi imposuit; et Andream fratrem ejus, qui erat discipulus Joannis; mittentes rete suum in mare, ut caperent pisces. Erant enim piscatores: quod utique officium futuro eorum officio spiritualiter congruebat, ut per piscium captionem figuraretur rationalium piscium in hoc mari magno et spatioso defluentium, utpote hominum adunatio per rete verborum cælestium.
paras.en: [[4:18|And Jesus walking by the sea of Galilee|Ambulans autem Jesus juxta mare Galilææ]], which by another name is called the lake of Genesareth; it was a great lake, according to Jerome, but it is called a sea after the custom of the Hebrew idiom, which calls any large gathering of waters a sea. He [[4:18|saw two brethren|Vidit duos fratres]], namely [[4:18|Simon who is called|Simonem, qui vocatur]] by another name [[4:18|Peter|Petrus]], that is, firm, and Cephas, that is, chief (both of which names Christ gave him), [[4:18|and Andrew his brother|et Andream fratrem ejus]], who was a disciple of John, [[4:18|casting a net into the sea|mittentes rete suum in mare]] to catch fish. [[4:18|for they were fishers|Erant enim piscatores]]: an office that was spiritually in keeping with their future office, so that by the catching of fish might be figured the gathering together, through the net of heavenly words, of rational fish, that is, of men, gliding about in this great and wide sea.

paras.t: Et ait illis: Venite post me, id est, gressibus corporis atque virtutibus animæ sequimini me, vos ipsos abnegando, et propria deserendo, ut evangelicæ perfectionis apicem apprehendatis; et faciam vos fieri, id est, constituam vos per gratiam apostolatus, piscatores hominum, id est collectores diversorum populorum infra unam Ecclesiam, per expansionem doctrinæ vestræ super eos, quemadmodum pisces diversi colliguntur per rete infra unam naviculam. Per rete ergo significatur verbum prædicationis; per navim, Ecclesia; per mare, mundus; per piscatorem, doctor seu prædicator; per piscationem, instructio, qua diversi in eadem fide, spe et caritate spiritualiter colliguntur. Juxta hanc similitudinem ait Dominus: Ecce ego mittam piscatores multos, et piscabuntur eos.
paras.en: [[4:19|And he saith to them: Come ye after me|Et ait illis: Venite post me]], that is, follow Me with the steps of the body and the virtues of the soul, denying yourselves and forsaking what is your own, that you may lay hold of the summit of gospel perfection; [[4:19|and I will make you to be|et faciam vos fieri]], that is, I will appoint you by the grace of the apostolate, [[4:19|fishers of men|piscatores hominum]], that is, gatherers of divers peoples into one Church, by spreading your teaching over them, as divers fish are gathered by a net into one little boat. By the net, then, is signified the word of preaching; by the ship, the Church; by the sea, the world; by the fisherman, the teacher or preacher; by the fishing, instruction, by which divers men are spiritually gathered together in the same faith, hope and charity. According to this likeness the Lord says: [[Jer 16:16|Behold I will send many fishers|Ecce ego mittam piscatores multos]], [[Jer 16:16|and they shall fish them|et piscabuntur eos]].

paras.t: At illi continuo relictis retibus, et ceteris quæ habebant, secundum quod alibi loquitur Petrus: Ecce nos reliquimus omnia; secuti sunt eum mente et corpore.
paras.en: [[4:20|And they immediately leaving their nets|At illi continuo relictis retibus]], and the other things they had (as Peter says elsewhere: [[Matt 19:27|Behold we have left all things|Ecce nos reliquimus omnia]]), [[4:20|followed him|secuti sunt eum]] in mind and in body.

paras.t: Triplex fuit discipulorum istorum vocatio: Una ad simplicem notitiam: quæ apud Joannem describitur. Quum enim Andreas a magistro suo Joanne Baptista audisset, Ecce Agnus Dei qui tollit peccata mundi, demonstrante Christum Joanne, Andreas secutus est Jesum, adduxitque Simonem fratrem suum ad eum. Ibi quoque describitur vocatio Philippi et Nathanael. Secunda vocatio fuit ad familiaritatem: quæ describitur apud Lucam, quando Petrus visa miraculosa piscium captione, procidit ad genua Jesu, dicens: Exi a me, Domine, quia homo peccator sum. Tunc enim omnia reliquerunt ad tempus, et rursus ad piscandum reversi sunt sicut et ante. Tertia fuit ad apostolatum, quando simpliciter omnia reliquerunt: et ista describitur hic. Illæ autem duæ vocationes Joanni et Jacobo filiis Zebedæi exhibitæ sunt simul cum Petro et Andrea. Unde nunc subditur:
paras.en: The calling of these disciples was threefold. The first was to simple acquaintance, which is described in John. For when Andrew had heard his master John the Baptist say, [[John 1:29|Behold the Lamb of God|Ecce Agnus Dei]], [[John 1:29|who taketh away the sin of the world|qui tollit peccata mundi]], as John pointed out Christ, Andrew followed Jesus, and brought his brother Simon to Him. There too the calling of Philip and Nathanael is described. The second calling was to familiar companionship, which is described in Luke, when Peter, on seeing the miraculous catch of fish, fell down at Jesus’ knees, saying: [[Luke 5:8|Depart from me|Exi a me]], [[Luke 5:8|O Lord|Domine]], [[Luke 5:8|for I am a sinful man|quia homo peccator sum]]. For then they left all things for a time, and went back to fishing again as before. The third was to the apostolate, when they left all things outright; and this is the one described here. Those two callings were given to John and James, the sons of Zebedee, together with Peter and Andrew. Hence it is now added:

paras.t: Et procedens inde, id est, Jesus ultra paululum tendens, vidit alios duos fratres, Jacobum Zebedæi filium, et Joannem evangelistam fratrem ejus, in navi cum Zebedæo patre eorum, reficientes, id est, reparantes et meliorantes, retia sua; et vocavit eos, forte per eadem verba quæ dixit ad Petrum et Andream, videlicet: Venite post me, faciam vos piscatores hominum. Joannes autem et Jacobus consanguinei erant Christi, videlicet filii sororis virginis benedictæ Mariæ. Illi autem statim relictis retibus et patre suo Zebedæo, secuti sunt eum, corde devoto et corpore prompto. Referunt multi, videnturque Hieronymus et Beda hoc sentire, Joannem istum fuisse sponsum in cujus nuptiis Christus convertit aquam in vinum, et quod Christus tunc vocaverit eum ad suum discipulatum, ita quod sponsam suam nunquam cognovit: sicque Joannes ter vocatus fuisset a Christo.
paras.en: [[4:21|And going on from thence|Et procedens inde]], that is, Jesus going a little further, [[4:21|he saw other two brethren, James the son of Zebedee|vidit alios duos fratres, Jacobum Zebedæi filium]], [[4:21|and John|et Joannem]] the evangelist, [[4:21|his brother, in a ship with Zebedee their father, mending|fratrem ejus, in navi cum Zebedæo patre eorum, reficientes]], that is, repairing and putting in better order, [[4:21|their nets: and he called them|retia sua; et vocavit eos]], perhaps with the same words that He said to Peter and Andrew, namely: [[4:19|Come ye after me|Venite post me]], [[4:19|I will make you|faciam vos]] [[4:19|fishers of men|piscatores hominum]]. Now John and James were kinsmen of Christ, namely sons of the sister of the blessed Virgin Mary. [[4:22|And they forthwith left their nets and father|Illi autem statim relictis retibus et patre]] Zebedee, [[4:22|and followed him|secuti sunt eum]] with devout heart and ready body. Many relate, and Jerome and Bede seem to hold, that this John was the bridegroom at whose wedding Christ turned water into wine, and that Christ then called him to be His disciple, so that he never knew his bride; and thus John would have been called by Christ three times.

paras.t: Et circuibat Jesus cum discipulis suis totam Galilæam, eundo de una civitate in aliam, docens in synagogis eorum, id est in domibus deputatis cultui Dei et actibus religiosis. Quamvis enim Judæi non habebant nisi unum templum, in quo secundum legem sacrificia immolabant, singulæ tamen urbes habebant synagogam, in quam convenerunt horis statutis ad laudandum Deum, ad legendum in lege et Prophetis, ad docendum, orandum ac audiendum salubria. Et prædicans Evangelium regni, id est doctrinam novæ legis ac gratiæ: in qua doctrina proponitur regnum cæleste pro præmio, quod Christus docuit appropinquare, et in se credentibus mox esse præstandum. Excessit enim doctrinam Mosaicam atque propheticam. Et quia doctrina Christi nova fuit et supernaturalis, omnem humanam rationem transcendens, et invisibilia bona pro mercede proponens, oportuit eam confirmari miraculis, tanquam divinæ veritatis argumentis et Dei sigillis, ut sciretur verus et a Deo missus esse talia prædicans. Quemadmodum etiam veritas naturalis scientiæ per principia prima probatur, et per rationes ex primis principiis per modum conclusionum deductas; sic veritas fidei, per opera miraculosa soli Deo possibilia roboratur et a Deo esse ostenditur, qui falsitatis confirmator ac testis esse non valet. Idcirco dicit Salvator: Opera quæ dedit mihi Pater, testimonium perhibent de me. Hinc ergo descripta Christi nova admirabilique doctrina, quæ tamen infra plenius introducitur, de ejus miraculis subinfertur: Et sanans omnem languorem inveteratum seu gravem, vel naturaliter incurabilem, et omnem infirmitatem minorem et per artem seu viam naturæ curabilem, qualis fuit cæcitas Tobiæ, in populo ad ipsum pro remedio humiliter accedente. Non tamen simpliciter omnes infirmos Judææ vel Galilææ curasse videtur, quum ejus discipuli post resurrectionem ipsius multos infirmos curaverint in Judæa et Galilæa, qui ante Christi passionem infirmi fuerunt.
paras.en: [[4:23|And Jesus went about|Et circuibat Jesus]] with His disciples [[4:23|all Galilee|totam Galilæam]], going from one city to another, [[4:23|teaching in their synagogues|docens in synagogis eorum]], that is, in houses set apart for the worship of God and for religious acts. For although the Jews had only one temple, in which they offered sacrifices according to the law, yet each city had a synagogue, in which they came together at fixed hours to praise God, to read in the law and the Prophets, to teach, to pray and to hear wholesome things. [[4:23|and preaching the gospel of the kingdom|Et prædicans Evangelium regni]], that is, the teaching of the new law and of grace, in which teaching the heavenly kingdom is set forth as the reward, which Christ taught was at hand and would soon be granted to those who believe in Him. For it surpassed the teaching of Moses and of the prophets. And because the teaching of Christ was new and supernatural, transcending all human reason and setting forth invisible goods as its reward, it had to be confirmed by miracles, as by proofs of divine truth and seals of God, so that one who preached such things might be known to be truthful and sent by God. Just as the truth of natural science is proved by first principles, and by reasonings drawn from first principles by way of conclusions, so the truth of faith is strengthened, and shown to be from God, by miraculous works possible to God alone, who cannot be the confirmer of falsehood or its witness. Therefore the Saviour says: [[John 5:36|the works which the Father hath given me|Opera quæ dedit mihi Pater]], [[John 5:36|give testimony of me|testimonium perhibent de me]]. Having described, then, the new and wonderful teaching of Christ (which is, however, set forth more fully below), he next adds concerning His miracles: [[4:23|and healing all manner of sickness|Et sanans omnem languorem]], long-standing or grave, or naturally incurable, [[4:23|and every infirmity|et omnem infirmitatem]], lesser and curable by art or by the way of nature, such as was the blindness of Tobias, [[4:23|among the people|in populo]] who came to Him humbly for a remedy. Yet He does not seem to have cured absolutely all the sick of Judea or Galilee, since after His resurrection His disciples cured many sick people in Judea and Galilee who had been sick before Christ’s passion.

paras.t: Et abiit opinio ejus, id est, fama et rumor de Christo divulgatus est, in totam Syriam, quæ est regio propinqua Galilææ. Crebra namque et magna prodigia fecerunt eum famosum. Et obtulerunt ei omnes male habentes, videlicet variis languoribus intus latentibus, et tormentis foris apparentibus comprehensos, et qui dæmonia habebant, id est a dæmonibus obsessos, et lunaticos. Lunatici nuncupantur, qui singulis vexantur lunationibus, et mente laborant: et accidit dum luna est plena. Lunatio autem est tempus quo luna recedit a sole, et rursus sequitur eum. Denique, secundum Hieronymum, tales non vere lunatici sunt, sed putantur lunatici propter fallaciam dæmonum, qui observantes lunaria tempora, creaturam, videlicet lunam, diffamare cupiebant, quasi ipsa causaret hujusmodi mala, ut in Creatorem blasphemiæ redundarent, tanquam qui tam nociva sidera condidisset. Sumit ergo Hieronymus lunaticos secundum intentionem eorum qui ab influxu lunæ ipsos vexari dixerunt. Et paralyticos, id est contractos morbo qui vocatur paralysis. Et curavit eos. Quos autem corpore sanavit, creditur curasse in anima, quoniam Dei perfecta sunt opera: quamvis multi eorum recidivaverint.
paras.en: [[4:24|And his fame went|Et abiit opinio ejus]], that is, the fame and report of Christ was spread abroad, [[4:24|throughout all Syria|in totam Syriam]], which is a region near Galilee; for frequent and great wonders made Him famous. [[4:24|and they presented to him all sick people|Et obtulerunt ei omnes male habentes]], namely those [[4:24|that were taken with divers diseases|variis languoribus]] lurking within [[4:24|and torments|et tormentis]] appearing without, [[4:24|and such as were possessed by devils|et qui dæmonia habebant]], that is, those beset by demons, [[4:24|and lunatics|et lunaticos]]. They are called lunatics who are troubled at each lunation and suffer in mind, and this happens when the moon is full. A lunation is the time in which the moon draws away from the sun and follows it again. But according to Jerome such people are not truly lunatic, but are thought lunatic because of the deceit of the demons, who, watching the times of the moon, wished to bring a creature, namely the moon, into ill repute, as though it caused such evils, so that blasphemies might redound upon the Creator, as having made such harmful stars. Jerome, then, takes “lunatics” according to the meaning of those who said that they were troubled by the influence of the moon. [[4:24|and those that had the palsy|Et paralyticos]], that is, those drawn up by the disease called paralysis, [[4:24|and he cured them|Et curavit eos]]. And those whom He healed in body, He is believed to have cured in soul as well, since [[Deut 32:4|The works of God are perfect|Dei perfecta sunt opera]], although many of them fell back again.

paras.t: Et secutæ sunt eum turbæ multæ de Galilæa et de Decapoli, id est provincia decem urbes continente. Decapolis namque dicitur a δέκα, quod est decem, et πόλις, civitas, quasi regio decem civitatum. Et de Jerosolymis, et de Judæa, id est ceteris urbibus quarum metropolis est Jerosolyma, et de trans Jordanem, id est de terra duarum tribuum et dimidiæ, utpote Ruben, Gad, et Manasse: quæ terra fuit ultra Jordanem respectu Judææ et Galilææ. Horum aliqui sequebantur Salvatorem propter informationem, sicut discipuli; aliqui propter curationem, ut languidi; aliqui propter cibum corporalem, ut famelici; aliqui ut signa viderent, quemadmodum curiosi; aliqui ut occasionem calumniandi invenirent, ut Scribæ et Pharisæi.
paras.en: [[4:25|And much people followed him from Galilee, and from Decapolis|Et secutæ sunt eum turbæ multæ de Galilæa et de Decapoli]], that is, the province containing ten cities; for Decapolis is so called from δέκα, which is “ten”, and πόλις, “city”, as it were the region of ten cities. [[4:25|and from Jerusalem, and from Judea|Et de Jerosolymis, et de Judæa]], that is, the other cities of which Jerusalem is the chief city, [[4:25|and from beyond the Jordan|et de trans Jordanem]], that is, from the land of the two tribes and a half, namely Ruben, Gad and Manasses, which land lay beyond the Jordan with respect to Judea and Galilee. Of these some followed the Saviour for instruction, as the disciples; some for healing, as the sick; some for bodily food, as the hungry; some to see signs, as the curious; some to find occasion for calumny, as the Scribes and Pharisees.

paras.t: Circa vocationem prædictorum quatuor Apostolorum, dicit Hieronymus: Piscatores et illitterati eliguntur et mittuntur ad prædicandum, ne fides credentium, non virtute Dei, sed eloquentia et doctrina fieri putaretur.
paras.en: On the calling of the four Apostles just mentioned, Jerome says: Fishermen and unlettered men are chosen and sent to preach, lest the faith of believers should be thought to come about not by the power of God but by eloquence and learning.

paras.t: Mystice autem, per Simonem Petrum signantur obedientes et firmi in fide, Simon quippe interpretatur obediens, Petrus dicitur firmus; per Joannem, speciali gratia decorati, Joannes enim interpretatur habens gratiam; per Jacobum, supplantantes peccata, quia Jacobus interpretatur supplantator. Per Andream, qui interpretatur virilis, designantur magnanimitate fulgentes, in quorum conspectu ad nihilum deductus est malignus. Hos tales vocat et mittit Salvator ad prædicandum, ad docendum, ad præsidendum. Oportet enim omnino ut dignus et efficax prædicator, doctor, sive prælatus, sit rectæ rationi, Deo atque Ecclesiæ semper obediens, et firmus in fide, quatenus alios ad sanctam obedientiam, fideique immobilem firmitatem inducat. Oportet quoque ut speciali gratia adornetur, imo exuberet, quatenus de plenitudine ejus accipiant alii, scilicet purgationem, illuminationem, et perfectionem. Item necesse est ut vitiorum sit victor, quatenus quomodo alios docet, ipse in primis adimpleat, ne sibi dicatur: Qui alium doces, te ipsum non doces; et, Medice, cura te ipsum. Rursus necesse est ut sit virilis in omnibus, non pusillanimis, non ponderans ista terrena, non succumbens adversis, nec mortem formidans amore justitiæ.
paras.en: Mystically, Simon Peter signifies those who are obedient and firm in faith: for Simon is interpreted “obedient”, and Peter means “firm”. John signifies those adorned with special grace, for John is interpreted “having grace”; James, those who supplant sins, for James is interpreted “supplanter” [James is the same name as Jacob, who “supplanted” his brother Esau]. By Andrew, who is interpreted “manly”, are signified those who shine with magnanimity, in whose sight [[Ps 14:4|the malignant is brought to nothing|ad nihilum deductus est malignus]]. Such men the Saviour calls and sends to preach, to teach, to preside. For it is altogether needful that a worthy and effective preacher, teacher or prelate be always obedient to right reason, to God and to the Church, and firm in faith, so that he may lead others to holy obedience and to an immovable firmness of faith. It is needful too that he be adorned with special grace, nay, that he overflow with it, so that others may receive of his fullness, namely purgation, illumination and perfection [the three hierarchical acts of Dionysius the Areopagite, by which the higher orders pass on to the lower what they have received from God]. Again, he must be a conqueror of vices, so that what he teaches others he himself may first fulfil, lest it be said to him: [[Rom 2:21|Thou therefore, that teachest another, teachest not thyself|Qui alium doces, te ipsum non doces]]; and: [[Luke 4:23|Physician, heal thyself|Medice, cura te ipsum]]. Again, he must be manly in all things, not faint-hearted, not setting store by these earthly things, not giving way to adversity, nor fearing death for the love of justice.

paras.t: Postremo, quum actio Christi sit omnium nostrum instructio, per hoc quod ipse totam Galilæam tam sollicite circuivit, docentur prælati et prædicatores oves sibi commissas vigilanter circuire, visitare, docere, consolari, fovere per se ipsos, si congrue fieri possit, vel per idoneos vicarios, sicut et de religioso rege Josaphat scriptum est: Misit de principibus suis, et cum eis Levitas et sacerdotes, habentes librum legis; et circuibant cunctas urbes Juda, erudiebantque populum.
paras.en: Lastly, since the action of Christ is the instruction of us all, from His going about all Galilee so carefully prelates and preachers are taught to go about the sheep committed to them watchfully, to visit, teach, console and cherish them, in person if it can fittingly be done, or through suitable vicars; as is also written of the devout king Josaphat: [[2 Par 17:7|he sent of his princes|Misit de principibus suis]], [[2 Par 17:8|And with them the Levites|et cum eis Levitas]] and priests, [[2 Par 17:9|having with them the book of the law|habentes librum legis]]: [[2 Par 17:9|and they went about all the cities of Juda, and instructed the people|et circuibant cunctas urbes Juda, erudiebantque populum]].

5.title: Elucidatio capituli quinti: Videns autem Jesus turbas, ascendit in montem
5.title_en: Explanation of the fifth chapter: “And seeing the multitudes, he went up into a mountain”

paras.t: Quoniam Dominus noster Jesus Christus secundum omnium vaticinia Prophetarum salus et lux mundi est, doctor justitiæ, et evangelicæ institutionis legislator, idcirco quum opportunum adfuit tempus, fecit quod de se ipso prædictum erat, tradens evangelicam legem. Et quoniam lex omnibus danda est, aperte proponenda, et ad hominum correctionem ac perfectionem ordinanda, propterea videns Salvator copiosissimam turbam se sequentem, instructione indigentem, et vitiis oneratam, ascendit in montem, ut ab omnibus melius videretur, ac planius audiretur. Secundo, ut per montem sublimem, evangelicæ legis ac disciplinæ excellentia monstraretur: de cujus utique legis excellentia accipi potest illud Psalmistæ, Justitia tua sicut montes Dei. Tertio, ut demonstraret prædicatorem verbi Dei, virtutum altitudinem debere conscendere, juxta illud Isaiæ: Super montem excelsum ascende, tu qui evangelizas Sion. Denique, secundum Augustinum, in hoc sermone Domini continetur quidquid ad optimos pertinet mores, et ad christianæ conversationis perfectionem. Ideo prout Dominus dederit, diligentius immorandum est præsenti sequentibusque quibusdam capitulis.
paras.en: Since our Lord Jesus Christ, according to the prophecies of all the Prophets, is the salvation and light of the world, the teacher of justice, and the lawgiver of the gospel ordinance, therefore, when the fitting time had come, He did what had been foretold of Him, and gave the law of the gospel. And since a law must be given to all, set forth openly, and directed to the correction and perfecting of men, the Saviour, seeing a very great multitude following Him, in need of instruction and weighed down with vices, went up into a mountain, first, that He might be better seen by all and more plainly heard. Secondly, that by the lofty mountain the excellence of the gospel law and discipline might be shown: and of the excellence of this law that saying of the Psalmist may well be taken, [[Ps 35:7|Thy justice is as the mountains of God|Justitia tua sicut montes Dei]]. Thirdly, to show that the preacher of the word of God ought to climb to the height of the virtues, according to that saying of Isaias: [[Is 40:9|Get thee up upon a high mountain, thou that bringest good tidings to Sion|Super montem excelsum ascende, tu qui evangelizas Sion]]. Lastly, according to Augustine, this sermon of the Lord contains whatever belongs to the best morals and to the perfection of the Christian life. Therefore, as the Lord shall grant, we must dwell more carefully on the present chapter and on some of those that follow.

paras.t: Ait ergo: Videns autem Jesus oculo corporali, turbas, de quibus in fine præcedentis capituli dictum est: quas oculo intellectuali incessabiliter vidit. Nam anima Christi semper a principio suæ creationis, actu intellexit scientia visionis omnia quæ unquam fuerunt, sunt et erunt. Ascendit in montem quemdam Galilææ, videlicet in montem Thabor, vel alium aliquem, secundum Hieronymum; non in montem Oliveti, ut aliqui putaverunt. Cur autem in montem ascenderit, dictum est. Et quum sedisset in monte tanquam magister, ad quem pertinet sessio in docendo, accesserunt ad eum discipuli ejus, qui quasi ceteris perfectiores, magistrum perfectionis sequi valebant, et ei propinquius copulari. Et aperiens os suum. Per hanc circumlocutionem notatur magnitudo dicendorum. Itaque, Aperiens os suum, id est, per se ipsum atque in propria persona loquens, legemque tradens, qui olim per angelos et Prophetas loquebatur, et per Moysen legem proposuit, docebat eos, dicens. Non dicitur, quod docuit turbas, sed discipulos: quod quomodo intelligendum sit, mox ostendetur.
paras.en: He says, then: [[5:1|And seeing|Videns autem]] Jesus, with the eye of the body, [[5:1|the multitudes|turbas]] of which mention was made at the end of the preceding chapter: whom with the eye of the intellect He saw unceasingly. For the soul of Christ, always, from the beginning of its creation, actually understood by the knowledge of vision [scientia visionis: the knowledge by which a mind beholds things as actually existing, whether past, present or to come] all things that ever were, are, and will be. [[5:1|He went up into a mountain|Ascendit in montem]], a certain mountain of Galilee, namely Mount Thabor or some other, according to Jerome; not the Mount of Olives, as some have thought.
