Why He went up into a mountain has been said. [[5:1|And when he was set down|Et quum sedisset]] on the mountain as a master, to whom it belongs to sit when teaching, [[5:1|his disciples came unto him|accesserunt ad eum discipuli ejus]], who, being as it were more perfect than the rest, were able to follow the master of perfection and to be joined more closely to Him. [[5:2|And opening his mouth|Et aperiens os suum]]. By this roundabout phrase the greatness of what is to be said is marked. And so, [[5:2|opening his mouth|Aperiens os suum]], that is, speaking by Himself and in His own person, and giving the law, He who of old spoke by angels and Prophets and set forth the law by Moses, [[5:2|he taught them, saying|docebat eos, dicens]]. It is not said that He taught the multitudes, but the disciples: how this is to be understood will be shown presently.

paras.t: Beati pauperes spiritu, quoniam ipsorum est regnum cœlorum. In exordio hujus sacrosancti sermonis, docet unigenitus Filius Dei octo beatitudines. Oportet ergo advertere, quod virtutes et dona, fructus et beatitudines, in aliquibus conveniunt, et in aliquibus distinguuntur. Virtus enim et donum in hoc conveniunt, quod utrumque eorum est habitus; differunt tamen in hoc, quod dona perficiunt, et in operando expeditas reddunt virtutes, easque in dignitate excellunt, demptis virtutibus theologicis, quæ præstantiores sunt donis: unde virtutes sunt plures quam dona, quæ non sunt nisi septem. Beatitudo vero et fructus in hoc conveniunt, quod utrumque eorum est actus virtutis; sed beatitudo superaddit fructui rationem perfecti et eminentis, ita quod de ratione beatitudinis est, ut sit actus excellentis virtutis, ad rationem vero fructus sufficit, quod sit actus virtutis delectationem spiritualem habens annexam. Interdum autem fructus accipitur pro delectatione actus virtuosi, et beatitudo pro virtute seu habitu. Imo hoc loco quidam per beatitudines istas intelligunt ipsas virtutes: quamvis magis proprie per eas intelligantur actus. Beatitudo enim consistit in actu, non in habitu, secundum Peripateticos: tamen Platonici dixerunt eam in habitu consistere. Quemadmodum autem christiani doctores distinguunt virtutes, ita quod virtutes in summo gradu consistentes dicuntur divinæ, convenientes statui perfectorum, non incipientium, nec proficientium; sic Peripatetici tales virtutes vocabant heroicas. Platonici vero seu Stoici vocabant eas virtutes purgati animi, a passionibus et vitiis absoluti. Harum ergo virtutum actus præsertim beatitudines dicuntur. Quidam præterea asserunt beatitudines potius esse actus donorum, quam virtutum, quoniam dona excedunt virtutes. Sed hoc sic intelligendum opinor, quia virtutes non producunt elicitive ipsas beatitudines, nisi secundum quod dona perficiunt ipsas virtutes, ut sint promptæ ad operandum, et omne obstaculum cito facileque repellant.
paras.en: [[5:3|Blessed are the poor in spirit: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven|Beati pauperes spiritu, quoniam ipsorum est regnum cœlorum]]. At the opening of this most holy sermon the only-begotten Son of God teaches eight beatitudes. We must notice, then, that virtues and gifts [the seven gifts of the Holy Ghost], fruits and beatitudes agree in some respects and are distinguished in others. Virtue and gift agree in this, that each of them is a habit; but they differ in this, that the gifts perfect the virtues and make them ready in acting, and excel them in dignity, except the theological virtues, which are more excellent than the gifts: and so the virtues are more in number than the gifts, which are only seven. A beatitude and a fruit agree in this, that each of them is an act of virtue; but a beatitude adds to a fruit the character of something perfect and eminent, so that it belongs to the nature of a beatitude to be the act of an excellent virtue, while for the nature of a fruit it is enough that it be an act of virtue with spiritual delight joined to it. Sometimes, however, a fruit is taken for the delight of a virtuous act, and a beatitude for the virtue or habit. Indeed, in this place some understand by these beatitudes the virtues themselves, although more properly the acts are understood by them. For beatitude consists in act, not in habit, according to the Peripatetics; the Platonists, however, said that it consists in habit. And just as the Christian doctors distinguish the virtues, so that the virtues that stand at the highest degree are called divine, as befitting the state of the perfect, not of beginners nor of those making progress, so the Peripatetics called such virtues heroic, while the Platonists, or Stoics, called them virtues of the purged soul, set free from passions and vices. It is the acts of these virtues above all, then, that are called beatitudes. Some, moreover, assert that the beatitudes are acts of the gifts rather than of the virtues, because the gifts surpass the virtues. But this, I think, is to be understood thus: that the virtues do not elicit the beatitudes [that is, produce them as their immediate source] except so far as the gifts perfect the virtues themselves, so that they are prompt to act and drive back every obstacle quickly and easily.

paras.t: De prima ergo et fundamentali beatitudine Veritas ait: Beati pauperes spiritu. In qualibet beatitudine duo tanguntur, videlicet meritum et præmium. Meritum est ipsa beatitudo viæ, videlicet actus virtutis: quod tangitur quum dicitur, Beati, etc. Præmium vero est merces merito correspondens: quæ tangitur quum dicitur, Quoniam, etc. Quum enim actus virtutis in hac vita sit laboriosus aliquo modo, maxime in principio (ars namque et virtus sunt circa difficilia, secundum Philosophum), idcirco Salvator beatitudines commendans, protinus subdit de præmio, ut ad beatitudines exercendas nos excitet. Commemoratio enim mercedis provocat et confortat laborantem. Expedit insuper scire, quod beatitudo est duplex, videlicet viæ et patriæ. Beatitudo viæ, est meritum seu actio virtuosa, unde jam sermo; beatitudo patriæ, est præmium cœleste. Beatitudo quoque habetur dupliciter, scilicet in spe et in re. Beatitudo ergo patriæ nunc habetur in spe, per hoc quod beatitudo viæ habetur in re. Hæc est enim dispositio propinqua et summa ad illam.
paras.en: Of the first and fundamental beatitude, then, the Truth says: [[5:3|Blessed are the poor in spirit|Beati pauperes spiritu]]. In each beatitude two things are touched on, namely merit and reward. The merit is the beatitude of the way itself, that is, the act of virtue: and this is touched on when it is said, [[5:3|Blessed|Beati]], etc. The reward is the recompense answering to the merit: and this is touched on when it is said, [[5:3|for|Quoniam]], etc. For since the act of virtue in this life is in some way laborious, above all at the beginning (for art and virtue are about difficult things, according to the Philosopher), the Saviour, in commending the beatitudes, at once adds something about the reward, to rouse us to practise the beatitudes. For the mention of the recompense spurs on and strengthens the one who labours. It is useful to know, moreover, that beatitude is twofold, namely of the way and of the fatherland [via, the way of this present life; patria, the heavenly fatherland]. The beatitude of the way is merit, or virtuous action, of which we are now speaking; the beatitude of the fatherland is the heavenly reward. Beatitude is also had in two ways, namely in hope and in fact. The beatitude of the fatherland, then, is now had in hope, by this, that the beatitude of the way is had in fact. For this is the nearest and highest disposition to that.

paras.t: Præterea, quum beatitudo stricte accepta sit optima operatio perfectissimæ virtutis, oportet quod inter octo beatitudines, sit una summa et essentialiter beatitudo vocata, præsertim quum in omni genere et ordinata multitudine, sit unum primum atque præcipuum, ad quod alia ordinantur. Hæc autem beatitudo in via est munditia cordis, in patria vero est visio Dei, qui ponitur tota merces. Ad munditiam ergo cordis aliæ beatitudines disponunt ac referuntur. Ex quo patet, quod beatitudines non enumerantur hoc loco secundum ordinem dignitatis seu perfectionis, quo eminentiora ac meliora priora vocantur; sed partim secundum ordinem generationis, quo imperfectum præcedit perfectum. Juxta quem modum dicit Apostolus: Non prius quod spirituale, sed quod animale; deinde quod spirituale.
paras.en: Furthermore, since beatitude taken strictly is the best operation of the most perfect virtue, among the eight beatitudes there must be one that is highest and is called beatitude in its essence, especially since in every genus and ordered multitude there is one thing first and chief, to which the others are ordered. This beatitude, in the way, is cleanness of heart; in the fatherland it is the vision of God, who is set down as the whole reward. To cleanness of heart, then, the other beatitudes dispose and are referred. From this it is plain that the beatitudes are not listed here according to the order of dignity or perfection, by which the more eminent and better things are called first, but partly according to the order of generation, by which the imperfect goes before the perfect. In this way the Apostle says: [[1 Cor 15:46|that was not first which is spiritual, but that which is natural: afterwards that which is spiritual|Non prius quod spirituale, sed quod animale; deinde quod spirituale]].

paras.t: Primam autem beatitudinem, quæ dicitur, Beati pauperes spiritu, Hieronymus, Augustinus et Chrysostomus exponunt de humilitate, ut sit sensus: Beati pauperes spiritu, id est humiles corde, qui non inflantur, non magna de se ipsis præsumunt, nec aliquid boni sibi, sed totum Deo attribuunt, pensantes illud Apostoli: Quid habes quod non accepisti? Et illud: Qui se putat aliquid esse, quum nihil sit, ipse se seducit. De quibus ait Psalmista: Humiles spiritu salvabit. Qui autem in propriis oculis magni et sapientes, ceterisque perfectiores sunt, non sunt pauperes spiritu. — Ambrosius vero et Leo Papa exponunt de voluntaria paupertate, propter Deum assumpta, desiderata, vel complacente, ut sit sensus: Beati sunt jam in spe, imo et beati in re, loquendo de beatitudine viæ, pauperes, id est temporalibus bonis carentes, spiritu, id est cum affectu cordis, ita quod divitias non appetunt, sed contemnunt, et in paupertate sua lætantur, nil proprium possidentes; dicentes cum Paulo: Omnia arbitror ut stercora, ut Christum lucrifaciam. Hæc est paupertas evangelica, quam consulit Christus, dicendo: Qui non renuntiat omnibus quæ possidet, non potest esse meus discipulus; itemque, Si vis perfectus esse, vade, et vende omnia quæ habes, et da pauperibus. Hæc est paupertas illa ditissima de qua Apostolus loquitur: Altissima paupertas eorum abundavit in divitias simplicitatis eorum. Hæc quoque est paupertas potentissima de qua Petrus claudo nato: Argentum, ait, et aurum non est mihi; quod autem habeo, hoc tibi do: In nomine Jesu surge et ambula. De utrisque autem pauperibus intelligi potest illud Isaiæ: Domine Deus, confitebor tibi, quia factus es fortitudo pauperi et egeno in tribulatione sua. Hæc ergo paupertas contemnit omnia exteriora, honores atque divitias, quantum possibile est: quatenus summo enti, in quo omnia bona, omnia pulchra ac desiderabilia superplenissime continentur, absoluta, tota et libera mente adhæreat homo, qui tanto minus Deo conjungitur, quanto amplius transitoriis implicatur, et per diversa distrahitur. O amanda, veneranda, et amplectenda paupertas! Cujus se Christus dedit exemplum, propter nos pauper factus, quum esset dives, secundum quod ait: Volucres cœli nidos habent, et vulpes foveas; Filius autem hominis non habet ubi caput reclinet. — Denique secundum utramque expositionem, paupertas spiritus est basis seu fundamentum beatitudinum ceterarum. Humilitas enim est radix, custos, et stabilimentum virtutum et omnis perfectionis. Similiter divitiarum abjectio efficit hominem ad omnia spiritualia expeditum, cœlestiumque gratiarum abundanter capacem.
paras.en: The first beatitude, which reads, [[5:3|Blessed are the poor in spirit|Beati pauperes spiritu]], Jerome, Augustine and Chrysostom expound of humility, so that the sense is: [[5:3|Blessed are the poor in spirit|Beati pauperes spiritu]], that is, the humble of heart, who are not puffed up, who presume no great things of themselves, and attribute no good to themselves but all to God, weighing that saying of the Apostle: [[1 Cor 4:7|what hast thou that thou hast not received|Quid habes quod non accepisti]]? And this: [[Gal 6:3|if any man think himself to be some thing, whereas he is nothing, he deceiveth himself|se putat aliquid esse, quum nihil sit, ipse se seducit]]. Of these the Psalmist says: [[Ps 33:19|he will save the humble of spirit|Humiles spiritu salvabit]]. But those who are great and wise in their own eyes, and more perfect than the rest, are not poor in spirit. — Ambrose, however, and Pope Leo expound it of voluntary poverty, taken up, desired, or gladly embraced for God’s sake, so that the sense is: [[5:3|Blessed|Beati]] are they already in hope, nay, blessed also in fact, speaking of the beatitude of the way, [[5:3|the poor|pauperes]], that is, those who lack temporal goods, [[5:3|in spirit|spiritu]], that is, with the affection of the heart, so that they do not seek riches but despise them, and rejoice in their poverty, possessing nothing of their own; saying with Paul: I [[Phil 3:8|count them but as dung, that I may gain Christ|arbitror ut stercora, ut Christum lucrifaciam]] [Denis reads Omnia arbitror, “I count all things”]. This is the gospel poverty that Christ counsels, saying: He [[Luke 14:33|that doth not renounce all that he possesseth cannot be my disciple|Qui non renuntiat omnibus quæ possidet, non potest esse meus discipulus]]; and again, [[Matt 19:21|If thou wilt be perfect, go sell what thou hast, and give to the poor|Si vis perfectus esse, vade, et vende omnia quæ habes, et da pauperibus]]. This is that richest poverty of which the Apostle speaks: [[2 Cor 8:2|their very deep poverty hath abounded unto the riches of their simplicity|Altissima paupertas eorum abundavit in divitias simplicitatis eorum]]. This, too, is that most powerful poverty of which Peter spoke to the man born lame: [[Acts 3:6|Silver and gold I have none|Argentum, ait, et aurum non est mihi]], he said, [[Acts 3:6|but what I have, I give thee. In the name of Jesus|quod autem habeo, hoc tibi do: In nomine Jesu]], [[Acts 3:6|arise and walk|surge et ambula]]. Of both kinds of poor that saying of Isaias may be understood: O Lord God, I will give glory to thee, because [[Is 25:4|thou hast been a strength to the poor|factus es fortitudo pauperi]] and to [[Is 25:4|the needy in his distress|egeno in tribulatione sua]]. This poverty, then, despises all outward things, honours and riches, as far as is possible, so that a man may cleave with a mind unbound, whole and free, to the highest Being, in whom all good things, all things beautiful and desirable, are contained in overflowing fullness; for a man is joined to God so much the less, the more he is entangled in passing things and drawn apart among many. O poverty, to be loved, revered and embraced! Of which Christ gave Himself as the example, having become poor for our sakes when He was rich, as He says: [[Matt 8:20|The foxes have holes, and the birds of the air nests|Volucres cœli nidos habent, et vulpes foveas]]; [[Matt 8:20|but the Son of man hath not where to lay his head|Filius autem hominis non habet ubi caput reclinet]]. — Finally, according to either exposition, poverty of spirit is the base or foundation of the other beatitudes. For humility is the root, the guardian and the stay of the virtues and of all perfection. Likewise the casting away of riches makes a man free and ready for all spiritual things, and abundantly able to receive heavenly graces.

paras.t: Deinde subditur præmium pauperum spiritu, seu merces voluntariæ paupertatis: quoniam ipsorum est regnum cœlorum, id est, cœlestis patriæ opulentia eis pro mercede debetur, atque parata est. Per regnum ergo cœlorum, plenissima omnium bonorum sufficientia designatur, de quibus Isaias et Paulus testantur, quia oculus non vidit, nec auris audivit, quæ præparavit Deus his qui diligunt illum. Quæ autem sunt bona hæc, nisi objectaliter ipsemet Deus gloriosus et felix, dives in se, et dives in aliis, qui erit omnia in omnibus? Formaliter vero sunt dotes animæ et corporis, et cetera quæ cœlestem beatitudinem ornant, complent, perficiunt. Quum enim præmium correspondeat merito, pauperibus et humilibus rite promittitur opulentia, atque sublimitas regni cœlestis.
paras.en: Then is added the reward of the poor in spirit, or the recompense of voluntary poverty: [[5:3|for theirs is the kingdom of heaven|quoniam ipsorum est regnum cœlorum]], that is, the wealth of the heavenly fatherland is owed to them as their recompense, and is made ready for them. By the kingdom of heaven, then, is signified the fullest sufficiency of all good things, of which Isaias and Paul bear witness that [[1 Cor 2:9|eye hath not seen, nor ear heard|oculus non vidit, nec auris audivit]] [[1 Cor 2:9|what things God hath prepared for them that love him|quæ præparavit Deus his qui diligunt illum]]. And what are these good things, if not, as their object, God Himself, glorious and blissful, rich in Himself and rich in others, who will be [[1 Cor 15:28|all in all|omnia in omnibus]]? Formally, however, they are the endowments of soul and body [dotes, the “dowries” of the glorified soul and body], and the other things that adorn, fill out and perfect the heavenly beatitude. For since the reward answers to the merit, the wealth and loftiness of the heavenly kingdom are fittingly promised to the poor and the humble.

paras.t: Beati mites, id est, qui omnem irrationabilem iram refrenant, et animo mansueto illatas adversitates atque injurias sustinent, nec propter aliquod contrarium occurrens irascuntur. Mititas nempe seu mansuetudo, est virtus moralis passionem iræ refrenans ac moderans. Nunc tamen præsertim fit mentio de mititate purgati animi, et sumitur mititas pro actu mititatis. Videtur autem mititas jam parum extensius accipi quam modo prædicto, videlicet prout patientiam, passionem tristitiæ ordinantem, includit, ut mites vocentur homines patientes, amaritudinis felle, et indignatione, et appetitu vindictæ carentes. Quemadmodum autem ira comparatur stultitiæ, quoniam actum rationis plurimum impedit, et inhonestos gestus in vultu ac corpore parit (propter quod Ecclesiastes dicit: Ne sis velox ad irascendum, quoniam ira in sinu stulti requiescit; et Job, Virum stultum interficit iracundia. Salomone quoque testante: Qui impatiens est, operatur stultitiam; et, Doctrina viri per patientiam noscitur); sic mititas maxime ornat scientiam, atque divinæ sapientiæ illustrationem meretur, faciens hominem veraciter sapientem, modestum, ornatum, secundum quod ait Psalmista, loquens de Deo: Diriget mansuetos in judicio, docebit mites vias suas. Et quoniam mititas sapientiam promeretur, et ad stabilem contemplationem disponit, impedimenta contemplationis, et causas internæ instabilitatis tollendo, videlicet iram, impatientiam, indignationem, et amaritudinem; ideo mites experiri merentur internæ pacis dulcedinem, juxta illud Psalmistæ: Mansueti autem hæreditabunt terram, et delectabuntur in multitudine pacis. Hæc etiam virtus specialem a Deo gratiam ac familiaritatem sortitur, imo et sublimationem ac beatitudinis altitudinem, prout fertur in Psalmo: Quia beneplacitum est Domino in populo suo, et exaltabit mansuetos in salutem. Facit quoque hominem proximis suis vehementer amabilem, sicut Ecclesiasticus scribit: Fili, in mansuetudine opera tua perfice, et super hominum gloriam diligeris. Hinc Jacobus ait in sua Canonica: Quis sapiens et disciplinatus inter vos? Ostendat ex bona conversatione operationem suam in mansuetudine sapientiæ. Unde Dionysius in epistola ad Demophilum monachum asserit, ideo Moysen, Joseph et David, maximam apud Deum gratiam invenisse, quoniam mansueti fuerunt.
paras.en: [[5:4|Blessed are the meek|Beati mites]], that is, those who curb all unreasonable anger, bear with a gentle mind the adversities and wrongs done to them, and are not angered by anything contrary that befalls them. For meekness, or mildness, is the moral virtue that curbs and moderates the passion of anger. Here, however, mention is made above all of the meekness of the purged soul, and meekness is taken for the act of meekness. Yet meekness seems to be taken here somewhat more widely than in the way just said, namely as it includes patience, which orders the passion of sorrow, so that those are called meek who are patient, free of the gall of bitterness, of indignation, and of the craving for revenge. And just as anger is likened to folly, because it greatly hinders the act of reason and breeds unseemly gestures in the face and body (for which reason Ecclesiastes says: [[Eccles 7:10|Be not quickly angry: for anger resteth in the bosom of a fool|Ne sis velox ad irascendum, quoniam ira in sinu stulti requiescit]]; and Job, Anger [[Job 5:2|killeth the foolish|Virum stultum interficit]] man; Solomon too bearing witness: [[Prov 14:17|The impatient man shall work folly|Qui impatiens est, operatur stultitiam]]; and, [[Prov 19:11|The learning of a man is known by patience|Doctrina viri per patientiam noscitur]]), so meekness above all adorns knowledge and merits the enlightening of divine wisdom, making a man truly wise, modest and well-ordered, as the Psalmist says, speaking of God: [[Ps 24:9|He will guide the mild in judgment: he will teach the meek his ways|Diriget mansuetos in judicio, docebit mites vias suas]]. And since meekness merits wisdom and disposes to steady contemplation, by taking away the hindrances of contemplation and the causes of inward unsteadiness, namely anger, impatience, indignation and bitterness, the meek therefore deserve to taste the sweetness of inward peace, according to that saying of the Psalmist: [[Ps 36:11|But the meek shall inherit the land, and shall delight in abundance of peace|Mansueti autem hæreditabunt terram, et delectabuntur in multitudine pacis]]. This virtue also obtains from God a special grace and familiarity, nay, exaltation and the height of beatitude, as is said in the Psalm: [[Ps 149:4|For the Lord is well pleased with his people: and he will exalt the meek unto salvation|Quia beneplacitum est Domino in populo suo, et exaltabit mansuetos in salutem]]. It also makes a man exceedingly lovable to his neighbours, as Ecclesiasticus writes: [[Ecclus 3:19|My son, do thy works in meekness, and thou shalt be beloved above the glory of men|Fili, in mansuetudine opera tua perfice, et super hominum gloriam diligeris]]. Hence James says in his Canonical Epistle: [[Jas 3:13|Who is a wise man and endued with knowledge, among you? Let him shew, by a good contestation, his work in the meekness of wisdom|Quis sapiens et disciplinatus inter vos? Ostendat ex bona conversatione operationem suam in mansuetudine sapientiæ]] [conversatio: manner of life]. Whence Dionysius, in his letter to Demophilus the monk, asserts that Moses, Joseph and David found the greatest favour with God because they were meek.

paras.t: Consequenter ponitur proportionatum præmium beatitudinis hujus: quoniam ipsi possidebunt in præsenti vita terram proprii corporis, id est, carnem suam habebunt rationis imperio subditam, compositam, gubernatam. Quum enim radio divinæ sapientiæ doceantur, se ipsos gubernant in omnibus. In futuro autem possidebunt terram, id est firmam et stabilem mansionem paradisi cœlestis, de qua Propheta: Credo videre bona Domini in terra viventium; et, Placebo Domino in regione vivorum. De qua in Isaia habetur: Si glorificaveris Dominum dum non invenitur voluntas tua, sustollam te super altitudinem terræ, dicit Dominus. Hoc est correspondens præmium mitium, utpote ne æstimemus in futuro mites sic posse repelli a terra cœlesti per invisibiles hostes, quomodo nunc frequenter expelluntur a terra elementari ac hæreditaria per hostes visibiles.
paras.en: Next is set down the reward proportioned to this beatitude: [[5:4|for they shall possess|quoniam ipsi possidebunt]] in the present life [[5:4|the land|terram]] of their own body [terra is both “land” and “earth”: Denis takes it first of the earth of the body, then of the heavenly land], that is, they shall have their flesh subject to the command of reason, ordered and governed. For since they are taught by the ray of divine wisdom, they govern themselves in all things. But in the future [[5:4|they shall possess the land|possidebunt terram]], that is, the firm and stable dwelling of the heavenly paradise, of which the Prophet says: [[Ps 26:13|I believe to see the good things of the Lord in the land of the living|Credo videre bona Domini in terra viventium]]; and, [[Ps 114:9|I will please the Lord in the land of the living|Placebo Domino in regione vivorum]]. Of which we read in Isaias: If thou [[Is 58:13|glorify|glorificaveris]] the Lord while [[Is 58:13|thy own will is not found|non invenitur voluntas tua]], [[Is 58:14|I will lift thee up above the high places of the earth|sustollam te super altitudinem terræ]], saith the Lord. This is the reward that answers to the meek, so that we should not think that in the world to come the meek can be driven from the heavenly land by invisible enemies in the way they are now often expelled from the earthly land of their inheritance by visible enemies.

paras.t: Convenienter præterea ponitur mititas post paupertatem spiritus. Primo, quoniam humiles et inopes faciliter contemnuntur ac injuriantur, et multas penurias atque incommoda sentiunt: idcirco in primis maxime indigent mititate, ne ad iram, vel impatientiam concitentur. Secundo, quoniam humiles ac pauperes maxime dispositi sunt ad mansuetudinem observandam, sicut superbi et cupidi ad iracundiam proni sunt, juxta illud: Ubi fuerit superbia, ibi et contumelia; ubi autem humilitas, ibi et sapientia.
paras.en: Meekness, moreover, is fittingly placed after poverty of spirit. First, because the humble and the needy are easily despised and wronged, and suffer many wants and hardships: therefore they above all have most need of meekness, lest they be stirred to anger or impatience. Secondly, because the humble and the poor are best disposed to keep meekness, just as the proud and the covetous are prone to wrath, according to that saying: [[Prov 11:2|Where pride is, there also shall be reproach: but where humility is, there also is wisdom|Ubi fuerit superbia, ibi et contumelia; ubi autem humilitas, ibi et sapientia]].

paras.t: Sequitur beatitudo tertia. Beati qui lugent, propria vel proximorum peccata deflendo, et ad patriam suspirando, vel Christo passo ac crucifixo compatiendo cordialiter. Sic luxit qui ait: Exitus aquarum deduxerunt oculi mei, quia non custodierunt legem tuam. Sic Samuel luxit Saulem, Jeremias Jerusalem, Daniel populi sui captivitatem. Sic ex desiderio patriæ luxit Apostolus, dicens: Infelix ego homo! quis me liberabit de corpore mortis hujus? Et Psalmista: Fuerunt mihi lacrimæ meæ panes die ac nocte, dum dicitur mihi quotidie, Ubi est Deus tuus; et denuo, Heu mihi! quia incolatus meus prolongatus est. Hic luctus omnem carnalem delectationem gustus et tactus, omnem inanem gloriationem in verbis, factis, et ludis abscindit, quemadmodum scriptum est: Renuit consolari anima mea. Et Ecclesiastes: Risum reputavi errorem; et gaudio dixi, Cur frustra deciperis? Videtur quoque hic luctus esse actus pœnitentiæ, vel caritatis fraternæ, sive divinæ, secundum quod diversæ sunt causæ ac species luctus. Aliqui vero infeliciter lugent propter damna temporalia.
paras.en: The third beatitude follows. [[5:5|Blessed are they that mourn|Beati qui lugent]], by weeping for their own sins or their neighbours’, by sighing for the fatherland, or by suffering with Christ, who suffered and was crucified, from the heart. So mourned he who said: [[Ps 118:136|My eyes have sent forth springs of water: because they have not kept thy law|Exitus aquarum deduxerunt oculi mei, quia non custodierunt legem tuam]]. So Samuel mourned for Saul, Jeremias for Jerusalem, Daniel for the captivity of his people. So the Apostle mourned out of longing for the fatherland, saying: [[Rom 7:24|Unhappy man that I am, who shall deliver me from the body of this death?|Infelix ego homo! quis me liberabit de corpore mortis hujus?]] And the Psalmist: [[Ps 41:4|My tears have been my bread day and night, whilst it is said to me daily: Where is thy God|Fuerunt mihi lacrimæ meæ panes die ac nocte, dum dicitur mihi quotidie, Ubi est Deus tuus]]; and again, [[Ps 119:5|Woe is me, that my sojourning is prolonged!|Heu mihi! quia incolatus meus prolongatus est]] This mourning cuts off every carnal delight of taste and touch, and every vain boasting in words, deeds and amusements, as it is written: [[Ps 76:3|My soul refused to be comforted|Renuit consolari anima mea]]. And Ecclesiastes: [[Eccles 2:2|Laughter I counted error: and to mirth I said: Why art thou vainly deceived?|Risum reputavi errorem; et gaudio dixi, Cur frustra deciperis?]] This mourning also seems to be an act of penance, or of brotherly charity, or of the love of God, according as the causes and kinds of mourning differ. But some mourn unhappily, for temporal losses.

paras.t: Præmium luctus est: quoniam ipsi consolabuntur per internam divinæ visitationis dulcedinem, sicut testatur Propheta: Secundum multitudinem dolorum meorum in corde meo, consolationes tuæ lætificaverunt animam meam. Consolantur autem in præsenti inchoative et aliqualiter, in patria vero complete atque totaliter. Si enim compatimur, et conglorificabimur. Pio etenim luctui sæpe miscetur, et pene semper eum concomitatur consolatio Spiritus Sancti, secundum illud: Domine, post tempestatem tranquillum facis, et post fletum exsultationem infundis. Vere enim et copiose meretur gustare quam dulcis est Dominus, ita ut cum admiratione exclamet: Quam magna multitudo dulcedinis tuæ, Domine! Qui hunc sanctum luctum assumit, omnia vana oblectamenta aspernatur, dicens cum Salomone: Melius est ire ad domum luctus quam ad domum convivii.
paras.en: The reward of mourning is: [[5:5|for they shall be comforted|quoniam ipsi consolabuntur]], by the inward sweetness of God’s visitation, as the Prophet bears witness: [[Ps 93:19|According to the multitude of my sorrows in my heart, thy comforts have given joy to my soul|Secundum multitudinem dolorum meorum in corde meo, consolationes tuæ lætificaverunt animam meam]]. They are comforted in the present life in a beginning and partial way, but in the fatherland completely and wholly. For [[Rom 8:17|if we suffer with him|Si enim compatimur]], we shall [[Rom 8:17|be also glorified with him|et conglorificabimur]]. For with holy mourning the consolation of the Holy Ghost is often mingled, and almost always goes with it, according to that saying: O Lord, [[Tob 3:22|after a storm thou makest a calm|post tempestatem tranquillum facis]], and after weeping [[Tob 3:22|thou pourest in joyfulness|exsultationem infundis]]. For truly and abundantly does he deserve to taste how sweet the Lord is, so that he cries out in wonder: [[Ps 30:20|O how great is the multitude of thy sweetness, O Lord|Quam magna multitudo dulcedinis tuæ, Domine]]! He who takes up this holy mourning spurns all vain delights, saying with Solomon: [[Eccles 7:3|It is better to go to the house of mourning, than to the house of feasting|Melius est ire ad domum luctus quam ad domum convivii]].

paras.t: Convenienter autem ordinatur beatitudo luctus tertio loco, quia post exteriorum abnegationem, et adeptam animæ mansuetudinem, aptus est homo ad considerationem eorum quæ præinductum pariunt luctum.
paras.en: And the beatitude of mourning is fittingly set in the third place, because after the renouncing of outward things and the gaining of meekness of soul, a man is fit to consider the things that bring forth the mourning just described.

paras.t: Sequitur quarta beatitudo. Beati qui esuriunt et sitiunt justitiam, id est, tam ardenti affectu appetunt in omnibus justitiam observari, ut Deus honoretur in omnibus, sicut famelicus appetit cibum et potum corporalem. Itaque esurire et sitire justitiam, quæ est virtus generalis, de qua nunc sermo, est vehementer optare ut omnes Deo obediant, et tam ipse quam alii in bona vita proficiant, unicuique quoque quod suum est, conferatur. De tali siti loquitur Isaias: Omnes sitientes, venite ad aquas; et Christus apud Joannem, Si quis sitit, veniat ad me. Hac fame et siti laborant homines religiosi, qui toto conatu student quotidie in gratia crescere, de virtute in virtutem procedere, et Deo semper cum ampliori reverentia deservire, secundum quod ait Apostolus: Ego non arbitror me apprehendisse; unum autem, quæ quidem priora sunt, obliviscens, in anteriora autem extendens me ipsum, ad destinatum sequor. Nemo autem tantum proficit, quantum desiderat, quatenus hoc ipsum quod agit, pro nihilo reputet, seque humiliet, et justitiam esurire nullo cesset in tempore. Quum enim fecerimus omnia quæ præcepta sunt nobis, dicere debemus: Servi inutiles sumus; quod debuimus facere, fecimus. Magna perfectio est ista esuries, quæ peccata consumit, quemadmodum ignis devorat stipulam.
paras.en: The fourth beatitude follows. [[5:6|Blessed are they that hunger and thirst after justice|Beati qui esuriunt et sitiunt justitiam]], that is, who desire with such burning affection that justice be kept in all things, that God may be honoured in all things, as a hungry man desires bodily food and drink. And so to hunger and thirst after justice, which is the general virtue [general justice: the virtue that directs the acts of every virtue to God and the common good, as distinct from justice as one particular virtue], of which we are now speaking, is to long vehemently that all should obey God, that both oneself and others should advance in good living, and that to each should be given what is his. Of such thirst Isaias speaks: [[Is 55:1|All you that thirst, come to the waters|Omnes sitientes, venite ad aquas]]; and Christ in John, [[John 7:37|If any man thirst, let him come to me|Si quis sitit, veniat ad me]]. With this hunger and thirst religious men labour, who strive with all their might daily to grow in grace, to go on from virtue to virtue, and to serve God ever with greater reverence, as the Apostle says: [[Phil 3:13|I do not count myself to have apprehended|Ego non arbitror me apprehendisse]]. [[Phil 3:13|But one thing|unum autem]]: forgetting the things that are past, and [[Phil 3:13|stretching forth myself|extendens me ipsum]] to those that lie ahead, [[Phil 3:14|I press towards the mark|ad destinatum sequor]] [Denis’s wording differs a little from the Vulgate: quæ quidem priora sunt, obliviscens, in anteriora autem extendens me ipsum]. But no one advances as far as he desires; and so let him count as nothing the very thing he does, humble himself, and never at any time cease to hunger after justice. For when we have done all things that are commanded us, we ought to say: [[Luke 17:10|We are unprofitable servants; we have done that which we ought to do|Servi inutiles sumus; quod debuimus facere, fecimus]]. A great perfection is this hunger, which consumes sins as fire devours stubble.

paras.t: Cujus præmium subditur: Quoniam ipsi sic esurientes saturabuntur. Nunc enim aliqualiter saturantur pane sacramentali, de quo ait Salvator, Caro mea vere est cibus, et sanguis meus vere est potus; pane quoque obedientiæ, de quo ait Joannes, Meus cibus est, ut faciam voluntatem Patris mei. Augetur enim in eis gratia Dei quotidie, quia quo aliquis magis se præparat gratiæ, eo copiosius eam sortitur. In futuro autem saturabuntur plenissime in intellectu atque affectu, quia tam clare Deum videbunt, possidebunt, ac diligent, sicut optabunt, eumque habendo obtinebunt quidquid optaverint. Propter quod dicit Psalmista: Adimplebis me lætitia cum vultu tuo; et, Satiabor quum apparuerit gloria tua.
paras.en: Its reward is added: [[5:6|for they|Quoniam ipsi]], thus hungering, [[5:6|shall have their fill|saturabuntur]]. For now they are in some measure filled with the sacramental bread, of which the Saviour says, [[John 6:56|my flesh is meat indeed: and my blood is drink indeed|Caro mea vere est cibus, et sanguis meus vere est potus]]; and also with the bread of obedience, of which John writes, [[John 4:34|My meat is to do the will of|Meus cibus est, ut faciam voluntatem]] my Father. For the grace of God is increased in them daily, since the more anyone prepares himself for grace, the more abundantly he receives it. But in the world to come they shall be filled most fully in intellect and affection, because they will see, possess and love God as clearly as they shall desire, and in having Him they will obtain whatever they have desired. For which reason the Psalmist says: [[Ps 15:11|thou shalt fill me with joy with thy countenance|Adimplebis me lætitia cum vultu tuo]]; and, [[Ps 16:15|I shall be satisfied when thy glory shall appear|Satiabor quum apparuerit gloria tua]].

paras.t: Porro ista esuries et sitis sequitur luctum prædictum: quia dum homo imperfectum suum conspicit, aliorum peccata perpendit, ad futuram felicitatem suspirat, aliud non exquirit nisi ut purgetur a culpa, tam ipse quam alii, crescat in gratia, et patriæ appropinquet jugiter per fervida desideria.
paras.en: Further, this hunger and thirst follows the mourning spoken of before: because when a man looks upon his own imperfection, weighs the sins of others, and sighs for the happiness to come, he seeks nothing else than that he and others alike be cleansed from guilt, that he grow in grace, and that he draw ever nearer to the fatherland by fervent desires.

paras.t: Beati misericordes, aliis compatiendo, subveniendo, ignoscendo, imo eorum miseriam quasi propriam æstimando ac relevando, corporales ac spirituales eleemosynas impertiendo. — Quorum præmium est: quoniam ipsi misericordiam consequentur, id est peccatorum remissionem, optatæ gratiæ infusionem, atque divinæ pietatis succursum in omnibus. Hoc est quod dicit Psalmista: Beatus qui intelligit super egenum et pauperem; in die mala liberabit eum Dominus. Ideo Salomon dicit: Per fidem et misericordiam purgantur peccata; et, Qui pronus est ad misericordiam, benedicetur. Tobias quoque instruens filium suum, sic eum hortatur: Quomodo potueris, ita esto misericors; et ne avertas faciem tuam ab ullo paupere: ita enim fiet, ut nec a te avertatur facies Domini. Plane misericordes rite censendi sunt, qui implent illud Apostoli: Quis infirmatur, et ego non infirmor? Quis scandalizatur, et ego non uror? Et rursus: Alter alterius onera portate. Hinc admonet Ephesios: Estote invicem benigni, misericordes, donantes invicem, sicut et Deus in Christo donavit vobis. Hac virtute Deo assimilamur, cui proprium est misereri et parcere.
paras.en: [[5:7|Blessed are the merciful|Beati misericordes]], by suffering with others, helping them, forgiving them, nay, by counting their misery as their own and relieving it, and by giving bodily and spiritual alms. — Their reward is: [[5:7|for they shall obtain mercy|quoniam ipsi misericordiam consequentur]], that is, the remission of sins, the pouring in of the grace they long for, and the help of God’s loving-kindness in all things. This is what the Psalmist says: [[Ps 40:2|Blessed is he that understandeth concerning the needy and the poor: the Lord will deliver him in the evil day|Beatus qui intelligit super egenum et pauperem; in die mala liberabit eum Dominus]]. Therefore Solomon says: [[Prov 15:27|By mercy and faith sins are purged away|Per fidem et misericordiam purgantur peccata]] [Denis has the two words the other way about: “by faith and mercy”]; and, [[Prov 22:9|He that is inclined to mercy, shall be blessed|Qui pronus est ad misericordiam, benedicetur]]. Tobias too, instructing his son, exhorts him thus: [[Tob 4:8|According to thy ability be merciful|Quomodo potueris, ita esto misericors]]; and [[Tob 4:7|turn not away thy face from any poor person: for so it shall come to pass that the face of the Lord shall not be turned from thee|ne avertas faciem tuam ab ullo paupere: ita enim fiet, ut nec a te avertatur facies Domini]]. Those are plainly to be reckoned merciful who fulfil that saying of the Apostle: [[2 Cor 11:29|Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is scandalized, and I am not on fire?|Quis infirmatur, et ego non infirmor? Quis scandalizatur, et ego non uror?]] And again: [[Gal 6:2|Bear ye one another's burdens|Alter alterius onera portate]]. Hence he admonishes the Ephesians: [[Eph 4:32|be ye kind one to another: merciful, forgiving one another, even as God hath forgiven you in Christ|Estote invicem benigni, misericordes, donantes invicem, sicut et Deus in Christo donavit vobis]]. By this virtue we are made like to God, whose property it is to have mercy and to spare [the words of the Church’s prayer, Deus, cui proprium est misereri semper et parcere].

paras.t: Beati mundo corde, hoc est puri in intellectu, et sinceri in voluntate, ita quod conscientiam peccati non habent, nec aliqua intentione obliqua fœdantur, sed contemplationi ac dilectioni Dei altissimi cœlestiumque bonorum vacant sine permixtione erroris, et absque occursu passionis animam obtenebrantis. Ad hanc cordis munditiam disponunt virtutes morales, appetitum sensitivum a passionum inordinatione purificantes, et ceteræ virtutes intellectuales, naturales, atque justitia, quæ est virtus specialis, moralis. Omnia enim hæc ordinantur ad hoc, ut intellectus dono sapientiæ supernaturalis supernaturaliter illustretur, donis quoque intellectus, scientiæ, et consilii; et ut voluntas divina caritate fervescat, donisque tribus, videlicet fortitudine, timore, et pietate perficiatur: quibus peractis, potens est anima stabiliter, sincere, et affectuose Deo vacare, contemplando ac diligendo. Sicque munditia cordis essentialiter est ardens contemplatio Dei, seu contemplativa ejus dilectio. Ad hanc cordis munditiam perducitur homo triplici via seu triplici actione hierarchica, utpote: purgativa, qua mundatur a culpa; illuminativa, qua divinitus illustratur, fitque sedes sapientiæ; et unitiva, seu perfectiva, qua caritate accensus Deo conjungitur.
paras.en: [[5:8|Blessed are the clean of heart|Beati mundo corde]], that is, pure in intellect and sincere in will, so that they have no consciousness of sin and are not defiled by any crooked intention, but give themselves to the contemplation and love of the most high God and of heavenly goods without admixture of error and without the onset of passion darkening the soul. To this cleanness of heart the moral virtues dispose, purifying the sense appetite from the disorder of the passions, and so do the other virtues, intellectual and natural, and justice, which is a special moral virtue. For all these are ordered to this, that the intellect be enlightened supernaturally by the gift of supernatural wisdom, and by the gifts of understanding, knowledge and counsel; and that the will glow with divine charity and be perfected by three gifts, namely fortitude, fear and piety: and when this has been done, the soul is able to give itself to God steadily, sincerely and with affection, contemplating and loving. And so cleanness of heart is, in its essence, the burning contemplation of God, or the contemplative love of Him. To this cleanness of heart a man is brought by a threefold way, or a threefold hierarchical action [in the language of Dionysius, the threefold work by which the hierarchies purify, enlighten and perfect]: namely the purgative, by which he is cleansed from guilt; the illuminative, by which he is enlightened by God and becomes a seat of wisdom; and the unitive, or perfective, by which, set on fire with charity, he is joined to God.

paras.t: Quum ergo puritas cordis sit finis omnium exercitiorum nostrorum, ac summa præsentis vitæ perfectio, debemus incessabiliter eam intendere, ad eam suspirare, ad ejus considerationem intellectum reducere, totiesque dolere ac resipiscere, quoties sentimus nos ab ea corruisse, recessisse, vel elongationem aliquam incurrisse. Propter quod Salomon monet: Omni custodia serva cor tuum, quia ex ipso vita procedit: et Moyses: Custodi temetipsum, et animam tuam sollicite; ne obliviscaris verborum Domini, et ne excidant de corde tuo cunctis diebus vitæ tuæ. Hoc Deo juvante facere possumus, si divini vultus præsentiam atque judicium sapienter pensemus, dicentes cum sancto Elia: Vivit Dominus, in cujus conspectu sto; et cum Psalmista, Meditatio cordis mei in conspectu tuo semper. Talis erat sanctus Job, dicens: Nonne Deus considerat vias meas, et omnes gressus meos dinumerat? Nec solum passiones et vitia magna, sed et cogitationes superfluæ et distractiones inanes, cordis tollunt aut minuunt puritatem, quia verissime ait Scriptura: Qui spernit modica, paulatim decidit. Oportet ergo omnem animi evagationem et cogitationem inutilem devitare, atque ad sortiendam cordis puritatem infatigabiliter vigilare, laborare, et exorare.
paras.en: Since, then, purity of heart is the end of all our exercises and the highest perfection of the present life, we ought to aim at it unceasingly, to sigh for it, to bring the mind back to the thought of it, and to grieve and amend as often as we feel that we have fallen from it, gone back from it, or drifted some way off from it. For which reason Solomon warns: [[Prov 4:23|With all watchfulness keep thy heart, because life issueth out from it|Omni custodia serva cor tuum, quia ex ipso vita procedit]]: and Moses: [[Deut 4:9|Keep thyself|Custodi temetipsum]], [[Deut 4:9|and thy soul carefully. Forget not the words|et animam tuam sollicite; ne obliviscaris verborum]] of the Lord, [[Deut 4:9|and let them not go out of thy heart all the days of thy life|et ne excidant de corde tuo cunctis diebus vitæ tuæ]]. This, with God’s help, we can do if we wisely weigh the presence and judgment of God’s countenance, saying with holy Elias: [[3 Kings 17:1|As the Lord liveth|Vivit Dominus]], [[3 Kings 17:1|in whose sight I stand|in cujus conspectu sto]]; and with the Psalmist, [[Ps 18:15|the meditation of my heart always in thy sight|Meditatio cordis mei in conspectu tuo semper]]. Such was holy Job, saying: Doth not God [[Job 31:4|consider my ways, and number all my steps|considerat vias meas, et omnes gressus meos dinumerat]]? Not only the passions and great vices, but also idle thoughts and empty distractions take away or lessen the purity of the heart, for most truly does Scripture say: [[Ecclus 19:1|he that contemneth small things, shall fall by little and little|Qui spernit modica, paulatim decidit]]. We must therefore shun every wandering of the mind and every useless thought, and watch, labour and pray without tiring to obtain purity of heart.

paras.t: Quoniam ipsi Deum videbunt facie ad faciem, id est clare per speciem: quæ visio beatifica correspondet munditiæ cordis.
paras.en: For [[5:8|they shall see God|Quoniam ipsi Deum videbunt]] [[1 Cor 13:12|face to face|facie ad faciem]], that is, clearly, by sight [per speciem, as opposed to “by faith”: compare 2 Corinthians 5:7]: and this beatific vision answers to cleanness of heart.

paras.t: Sequitur beatitudo septima. Beati pacifici, hoc est internæ pacis, fraternæ concordiæ, communisque unanimitatis amatores, sectatores, et operatores: qui primo in se ipsis pacem habere conantur, ut appetitus inferior superiori obediat, sensualitas rationi, et caro spiritui, et ipse totus homo obediat Deo; deinde cum aliis satagunt pacem habere, et discordantes reconciliare, omnesque ad unanimitatem quamdam reducere: quemadmodum in primitiva Ecclesia multitudinis credentium erat cor unum et anima una. Sic enim Deus habitare facit unius moris in domo. De qua habitatione concordi atque fraterna cantamus: Ecce quam bonum et quam jucundum, habitare fratres in unum! Hæc pax ex caritate procedit, juxta illud Psalmistæ, Pax multa diligentibus legem tuam; et per justitiam custoditur, sicut Isaias fatetur, Et erit opus justitiæ pax. De qua pace dicit Salvator: Pacem meam do vobis; non quomodo mundus dat, ego do vobis. Itemque Apostolus: Pax Christi, quæ exsuperat omnem sensum, custodiat corda vestra. Quod enim pax ista appetenda sit, præcipue omni Christiano, constat ex hoc quod Christus suos discipulos salutando dicere consuevit, Pax vobis; eisque præcepit: In quamcumque domum intraveritis, primum dicite, Pax huic domui. Idcirco ad hanc beatitudinem sæpe nos hortatur Apostolus: ut quum ait Ephesiis, Solliciti servare unitatem spiritus in vinculo pacis; et alibi, Si fieri (inquit) potest, quod ex vobis est, cum omnibus hominibus pacem habentes.
paras.en: The seventh beatitude follows. [[5:9|Blessed are the peacemakers|Beati pacifici]], that is, the lovers, followers and workers of inward peace, of brotherly concord and of common unity of mind: who first strive to have peace within themselves, so that the lower appetite obeys the higher, sensuality obeys reason and the flesh the spirit, and the whole man himself obeys God; and then are busy to have peace with others, to reconcile those at variance, and to bring all back to a certain unity of mind: as in the early Church [[Acts 4:32|the multitude of believers had but one heart and one soul|multitudinis credentium erat cor unum et anima una]]. For it is thus that God [[Ps 67:7|maketh men of one manner to dwell in a house|habitare facit unius moris in domo]]. Of this harmonious and brotherly dwelling we sing: [[Ps 132:1|Behold how good and how pleasant it is for brethren to dwell together in unity|Ecce quam bonum et quam jucundum, habitare fratres in unum]]! This peace proceeds from charity, according to that saying of the Psalmist, [[Ps 118:165|Much peace have they that love thy law|Pax multa diligentibus legem tuam]]; and it is guarded by justice, as Isaias declares, [[Is 32:17|And the work of justice shall be peace|Et erit opus justitiæ pax]]. Of this peace the Saviour says: [[John 14:27|my peace I give unto you: not as the world giveth, do I give unto you|Pacem meam do vobis; non quomodo mundus dat, ego do vobis]]. And likewise the Apostle: The peace of Christ, [[Phil 4:7|which surpasseth all understanding, keep your hearts|quæ exsuperat omnem sensum, custodiat corda vestra]] [the Vulgate has Pax Dei, “the peace of God”]. That this peace is to be sought, above all by every Christian, is plain from this, that Christ, in greeting His disciples, was wont to say, [[Luke 24:36|Peace be to you|Pax vobis]]; and He commanded them: [[Luke 10:5|Into whatever house you enter, first say: Peace be to this house|In quamcumque domum intraveritis, primum dicite, Pax huic domui]]. Therefore the Apostle often exhorts us to this beatitude: as when he says to the Ephesians, [[Eph 4:3|Careful to keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace|Solliciti servare unitatem spiritus in vinculo pacis]]; and elsewhere, [[Rom 12:18|If it be possible|Si fieri]] (he says), [[Rom 12:18|as much as is in you, have peace with all men|potest, quod ex vobis est, cum omnibus hominibus pacem habentes]].

paras.t: Præmium autem pacificorum subjungitur: quoniam filii Dei vocabuntur, hoc est adoptivi, et digni erunt vocari filii Dei in præsenti sæculo, et in futuro potissimum. Homines namque filii Dei vocantur propter aliquam assimilationem cum eo. Hoc autem maxime convenit Deo, amare et facere pacem, secundum illud Apostoli: Deus erat in Christo mundum reconcilians sibi. Et de Christo ait: Ipse enim est pax nostra, qui fecit utraque unum. Pacifici ergo sunt similes Deo, qui cum Psalmista dicere possunt: Cum his qui oderunt pacem, eram pacificus. Verumtamen, sicut dicit Chrysostomus, Multi sunt qui alios libenter reconciliant, et ipsi inimicis suis nunquam ex corde reconciliantur. Hi tales, illusores sunt pacis, non amatores.
paras.en: The reward of the peacemakers is added: [[5:9|for they shall be called the children of God|quoniam filii Dei vocabuntur]], that is, adopted children, and they will be worthy to be called children of God in the present age, and most of all in the age to come. For men are called children of God because of some likeness to Him. And this above all befits God, to love peace and to make it, according to that saying of the Apostle: God [[2 Cor 5:19|was in Christ, reconciling the world to himself|erat in Christo mundum reconcilians sibi]]. And of Christ he says: [[Eph 2:14|For he is our peace, who hath made both one|Ipse enim est pax nostra, qui fecit utraque unum]]. Peacemakers, then, are like God, and can say with the Psalmist: [[Ps 119:7|With them that hated peace I was peaceable|Cum his qui oderunt pacem, eram pacificus]]. Yet, as Chrysostom says, there are many who gladly reconcile others, and are themselves never reconciled from the heart with their own enemies. Such as these are mockers of peace, not lovers of it.

paras.t: Octava demum beatitudo subjungitur. Beati qui persecutionem patiuntur propter justitiam, hoc est propter veritatem doctrinæ, propter veritatem vitæ, vel propter veritatem justitiæ, scilicet propter fidem, bonam conversationem, vel æquitatis et juris defensionem: et hoc, ex amore Dei, ad ejus honorem et gloriam. Veritas enim et æquitas pariunt odium. Qui igitur propter nullam adversitatem et persecutionem relinquit viam justitiæ, ille beatus est, dicens cum sancto Job: Donec deficiam, non recedam ab innocentia mea, et justificationem quam cœpi, non deseram. Multi autem propter suos excessus castigantur, qui volentes se ipsos excusare et quasi beatificare, inconvenienter allegant istam scripturam, dicentes, Beati qui persecutionem patiuntur propter justitiam, quum ipsi condignam luant disciplinam propter suam malitiam. Verumtamen, si quis excessit, et pœnam sibi inflictam pro culpa sua æquanimiter tolerat, etiam ipse quodammodo beatus esse videtur. Quamvis enim non patitur propter justitiam suam, tanquam propter causam alios ad persequendum moventem, patitur tamen propter justitiam, tanquam propter causam finalem, videlicet ut sua culpa per pœnam ordinetur, et Dei injuria vindicetur, amissaque gratia reparetur. Idcirco quidquid adversitatis et pœnæ nobis acciderit, debemus propter nostra peccata patienter sufferre, reputantes hæc ipsa supplicia nostris flagitiis esse minora. Sed hoc multo minus est, quam propter justitiam pati. Unde Petrus inquit: Hæc est gratia, si propter conscientiam Dei sustinet quis tristitias, patiens injuste. Quæ enim gratia, si peccantes et colaphizati suffertis? Si autem benefacientes sustinetis, hæc est gratia apud Deum: in hoc enim vocati estis.
paras.en: Lastly the eighth beatitude is added. [[5:10|Blessed are they that suffer persecution for justice' sake|Beati qui persecutionem patiuntur propter justitiam]], that is, for the truth of doctrine, for the truth of life, or for the truth of justice, namely for the faith, for a good manner of life, or for the defence of equity and right: and this out of love of God, for His honour and glory. For truth and equity breed hatred. He, then, who for no adversity or persecution forsakes the way of justice is blessed, saying with holy Job: [[Job 27:5|till I die I will not depart from my innocence|Donec deficiam, non recedam ab innocentia mea]], and [[Job 27:6|My justification, which I have begun to hold, I will not forsake|justificationem quam cœpi, non deseram]]. But many are chastised for their own excesses, who, wishing to excuse themselves and as it were call themselves blessed, unfittingly allege this scripture, saying, [[5:10|Blessed are they that suffer persecution for justice' sake|Beati qui persecutionem patiuntur propter justitiam]], when they are paying a well-deserved chastisement for their own wickedness. Yet if someone has gone astray and bears with an even mind the punishment laid on him for his fault, he too seems in a certain way to be blessed. For although he does not suffer for his justice as for the cause that moves others to persecute him, he does suffer for justice as for the final cause, namely that his fault may be set in order by the punishment, the wrong done to God avenged, and the grace he lost restored. Therefore, whatever adversity and punishment befalls us, we ought to bear it patiently for our sins, reckoning these very torments to be less than our crimes. But this is much less than to suffer for justice. Whence Peter says: [[1 Pet 2:19|this is thankworthy|Hæc est gratia]] [gratia: “grace”, or “thanks”], [[1 Pet 2:19|if, for conscience towards God, a man endure sorrows, suffering wrongfully|si propter conscientiam Dei sustinet quis tristitias, patiens injuste]]. For what thanks is it, [[1 Pet 2:20|if, committing sin and being buffeted for it, you endure|si peccantes et colaphizati suffertis]]? [[1 Pet 2:20|But if doing well you suffer|Si autem benefacientes sustinetis]], [[1 Pet 2:20|this is thankworthy before God|hæc est gratia apud Deum]]: [[1 Pet 2:21|For unto this are you called|in hoc enim vocati estis]].

paras.t: Insuper taliter patientium præmium subditur: quoniam ipsorum est regnum cœlorum, id est, æternam victoriam consequentur. Oppressis enim atque afflictis, maxime convenit gloria regni, consolatioque cœlestis. Hoc præmium octavæ et ultimæ beatitudinis, primæ quoque beatitudini est promissum, quum dicitur: Beati pauperes spiritu, quoniam ipsorum est regnum cœlorum. Considerando nempe in regno cœlesti sublimitatem et opulentiam universorum bonorum, sic ponitur præmium paupertatis; considerando autem in eo plenitudinem gaudiorum, sic ponitur præmium patientium et afflictorum propter justitiam. Prædictarum autem beatitudinum præmia unum et idem sunt, vel essentialiter, vel reductive. Quid enim est regnum cœlorum, nisi possessio terræ viventium? Et quid est consolatio patriæ, nisi prædicta possessio, vel aliquid consequens eam? Similiter saturari et Deum videre, idem exsistunt. Hujus ultimæ beatitudinis ad martyres maxime pertinentis, omnes electi participes sunt, prout testatur Apostolus: Quia omnes qui volunt pie vivere in Christo, persecutionem patientur.
paras.en: Moreover, the reward of those who suffer in this way is added: [[5:10|for theirs is the kingdom of heaven|quoniam ipsorum est regnum cœlorum]], that is, they shall attain eternal victory. For to the oppressed and afflicted the glory of the kingdom and heavenly consolation are above all fitting. This reward of the eighth and last beatitude is promised to the first beatitude also, when it is said: [[5:3|Blessed are the poor in spirit: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven|Beati pauperes spiritu, quoniam ipsorum est regnum cœlorum]]. For when one considers in the heavenly kingdom the loftiness and wealth of all good things, it is set down as the reward of poverty; but when one considers in it the fullness of joys, it is set down as the reward of those who suffer and are afflicted for justice. The rewards of the beatitudes named are one and the same, either essentially or by reduction [that is, as things that are traced back to the one essential reward]. For what is the kingdom of heaven, if not the possession of the land of the living? And what is the consolation of the fatherland, if not that same possession, or something that follows from it? Likewise, to be filled and to see God are the same. In this last beatitude, which belongs above all to the martyrs, all the elect have a share, as the Apostle testifies: For [[2 Tim 3:12|all that will live godly in Christ|omnes qui volunt pie vivere in Christo]] [[2 Tim 3:12|shall suffer persecution|persecutionem patientur]].

paras.t: Consequenter Salvator quasi exponit beatitudinem ultimam. Beati estis quum maledixerint, id est, malum de vobis dixerint, homines, secundum modum qui subditur, scilicet propter Christum, et persecuti vos fuerint, mala inferendo, vel de loco ad locum fugando, et dixerint omne malum adversum vos, varia crimina vobis imponendo, non veraciter, sed mentientes, id est, mendaciter vos accusantes, propter me, id est, omnia mala hæc vobis inferentes ob id, quoniam mihi adhæretis ac ministratis, videlicet propter justitiam vestram. Gaudete interius, cordialiter delectando in istis adversis: quemadmodum dicit Apostolus, Gloriamur in tribulationibus; et exsultate, id est, ex plenitudine interioris jucunditatis signa lætitiæ foris ostendite: juxta illud, Cor meum et caro mea exsultaverunt in Deum vivum. Hoc est quod in Jacobo docetur: Omne gaudium existimate, fratres, quum in diversas tentationes incideritis. Hæc enim sunt magna beneficia Dei, sicut affirmat Apostolus, dicens: Vobis datum est pro Christo, non solum ut credatis in eum, sed etiam ut patiamini pro illo. Et Petrus: Si exprobramini, inquit, in nomine Christi, beati eritis. Hinc ait Salvator: In mundo pressuram habebitis; sed confidite, quia ego vici mundum.
paras.en: Next the Saviour, as it were, expounds the last beatitude. [[5:11|Blessed are ye when they shall revile you|Beati estis quum maledixerint]], that is, when men shall speak evil of you, in the manner that is added, namely for Christ’s sake, [[5:11|and persecute you|et persecuti vos fuerint]], by inflicting evils on you or by driving you from place to place, [[5:11|and speak all that is evil against you|et dixerint omne malum adversum vos]], laying various crimes to your charge, not truly but [[5:11|untruly|mentientes]], that is, accusing you falsely, [[5:11|for my sake|propter me]], that is, inflicting all these evils on you for this reason, that you cleave to Me and serve Me, namely for your justice. [[5:12|Be glad|Gaudete]] inwardly, delighting from the heart in these adversities: as the Apostle says, [[Rom 5:3|we glory also in tribulation|Gloriamur in tribulationibus]]; [[5:12|and rejoice|et exsultate]], that is, out of the fullness of inward gladness show signs of joy outwardly: according to that saying, [[Ps 83:3|My heart and my flesh have rejoiced in the living God|Cor meum et caro mea exsultaverunt in Deum vivum]]. This is what is taught in James: [[Jas 1:2|count it all joy|Omne gaudium existimate]], brethren, [[Jas 1:2|when you shall fall into divers temptations|quum in diversas tentationes incideritis]]. For these are great benefits of God, as the Apostle affirms, saying: [[Phil 1:29|unto you it is given for Christ, not only to believe in him, but also to suffer for him|Vobis datum est pro Christo, non solum ut credatis in eum, sed etiam ut patiamini pro illo]]. And Peter: [[1 Pet 4:14|If you be reproached|Si exprobramini]], he says, [[1 Pet 4:14|for the name of Christ, you shall be blessed|in nomine Christi, beati eritis]]. Hence the Saviour says: [[John 16:33|In the world you shall have distress|In mundo pressuram habebitis]]; [[John 16:33|But have confidence|sed confidite]], for [[John 16:33|I have overcome the world|ego vici mundum]].

paras.t: Quoniam merces vestra copiosa est in cœlis. Hoc est una ratio gloriandi in adversis, magnitudo remunerationis: quia testante Apostolo, Id quod in præsenti est momentaneum et leve tribulationis nostræ, supra modum in sublimitate æternum gloriæ pondus operatur in nobis. Unde Salvator ait discipulis suis: Vos nunc quidem tristitiam habetis; iterum autem videbo vos, et gaudebit cor vestrum, et gaudium vestrum nemo tollet a vobis. Quum ergo non sint condignæ passiones hujus temporis ad futuram gloriam, debemus in omni tribulatione cordialiter exsultare. Gaudendum quoque est in istis adversis propter alias causas, videlicet quia per eas Christo passo assimilamur, Deum veneramur, et sanctis hominibus conformamur. Ideo subditur: Sic enim, hoc est, etiam ideo in adversis et persecutionibus istis gaudete, quia persecuti sunt Judæi Prophetas, qui fuerunt ante vos, videlicet Isaiam, Jeremiam, et ceteros. Propter quod Stephanus ait: Quem Prophetarum non sunt persecuti patres vestri? Ex hoc patet, verba ista specialiter dici ad Apostolos ceterosque discipulos.
paras.en: [[5:12|For your reward is very great in heaven|Quoniam merces vestra copiosa est in cœlis]]. This is one reason for glorying in adversities, the greatness of the recompense: for, as the Apostle testifies, [[2 Cor 4:17|that which is at present momentary and light of our tribulation worketh for us above measure, exceedingly an eternal weight of glory|Id quod in præsenti est momentaneum et leve tribulationis nostræ, supra modum in sublimitate æternum gloriæ pondus operatur in nobis]]. Whence the Saviour says to His disciples: [[John 16:22|you now indeed have sorrow: but I will see you again and your heart shall rejoice. And your joy no man shall take from you|Vos nunc quidem tristitiam habetis; iterum autem videbo vos, et gaudebit cor vestrum, et gaudium vestrum nemo tollet a vobis]]. Since, then, [[Rom 8:18|the sufferings of this time are not worthy to be compared with the glory to come|non sint condignæ passiones hujus temporis ad futuram gloriam]], we ought in every tribulation to rejoice from the heart. We must rejoice in these adversities for other reasons too, namely because through them we are made like to Christ in His passion, we honour God, and we are conformed to holy men. Therefore it is added: [[5:12|For so|Sic enim]], that is, rejoice in these adversities and persecutions for this reason also, that the Jews [[5:12|persecuted the prophets that were before you|persecuti sunt Prophetas, qui fuerunt ante vos]], namely Isaias, Jeremias and the rest. For which reason Stephen says: [[Acts 7:52|Which of the prophets have not your fathers persecuted?|Quem Prophetarum non sunt persecuti patres vestri?]] From this it is plain that these words are said especially to the Apostles and the other disciples.

paras.t: Circa præinducta magna oritur quæstio, an sermo præsens, quem hoc loco describit Matthæus, sit idem cum sermone qui in Luca describitur. Ad hoc quidam dixerunt, quod imo, quia uterque sermo idem habet principium, eumdemque finem, et in multis intermediis coincidit. Alii tenent oppositum: primo, quoniam secundum Matthæum Christus prædicavit in monte, secundum Lucam autem descendit de monte, et prædicavit in loco campestri; secundo, quia secundum Matthæum prædicavit sedendo, secundum Lucam stando; tertio, quia secundum Matthæum docuit octo beatitudines, secundum Lucam quatuor; quarto, quoniam Lucas multa omittit quæ ponit Matthæus. — Quid horum sit verius, ignoratur. Utriusque tamen opinionis rationes satis faciliter solverentur. Primam namque opinionem tenendo, diceretur quod Christus primo cum discipulis montem ascendit; ibique electione Apostolorum facta, et prædicatione incepta, descendit versus pedem montis, et ibi stans docuit discipulos, et populum simul: et si mons ille fuit in campo, tunc utique stando circa montis ascensum, stetit in loco campestri. Nec obstat quod multa omittit Lucas, quæ ponit Matthæus: sicut in Oratione dominica Matthæus ponit septem petitiones, Lucas quinque dumtaxat; uterque tamen eorum eamdem orationem describit. Sciens enim unus Evangelista, aliquid ab alio plene digestum, minus prosequitur illud. Qui vero secundam opinionem tuetur, dicere potest, quod non sit inconveniens diversos sermones eodem modo inchoari ac terminari, atque in multis communicare. Hæc secunda opinio verior æstimatur a quibusdam, videlicet quod fuerint diversi sermones, sicut patescit diligenter conspicienti utriusque sermonis descriptionem.
paras.en: Concerning what has been set out, a great question arises: whether the present sermon, which Matthew describes in this place, is the same as the sermon described in Luke. To this some have said that it is, because both sermons have the same beginning and the same end, and agree in many things in between. Others hold the opposite: first, because according to Matthew Christ preached on the mountain, but according to Luke He came down from the mountain and preached in a level place; secondly, because according to Matthew He preached sitting, according to Luke standing; thirdly, because according to Matthew He taught eight beatitudes, according to Luke four; fourthly, because Luke leaves out many things that Matthew puts in. — Which of these is truer is not known. Yet the arguments of either opinion could be answered easily enough. For holding the first opinion, one would say that Christ first went up the mountain with His disciples; and there, having chosen the Apostles and begun to preach, He came down towards the foot of the mountain, and there, standing, taught the disciples and the people together: and if that mountain stood in a plain, then indeed, standing near the ascent of the mountain, [[Luke 6:17|he stood in a plain place|stetit in loco campestri]]. Nor is it an objection that Luke leaves out many things that Matthew puts in: just as in the Lord’s Prayer Matthew gives seven petitions and Luke only five, and yet both of them describe the same prayer. For one Evangelist, knowing that something has been fully set out by another, follows it up less. But he who defends the second opinion can say that there is nothing unfitting in different sermons beginning and ending in the same way and having many things in common. This second opinion, namely that there were different sermons, is judged the truer by some, as is clear to anyone who looks carefully at the description of each sermon.

5.title: Prosecutio expositionis præsentis capituli, ab eo loco quo dicitur: Vos estis sal terræ, etc.
5.title_en: Continuation of the exposition of the present chapter, from the place where it says: “You are the salt of the earth”, etc.

paras.t: Quamvis sermo iste ad turbas factus dicatur, ad Apostolos tamen præsertim directus est. In principio enim hujus capituli dicebatur : Accesserunt ad eum discipuli ejus, et aperiens os suum, docebat eos. Lucas etiam dicit : Elevatis oculis in discipulos suos, dixit, etc. Eosdem ergo nunc alloquens, docet quales debeant esse, tam ipsi quam eorum successores, videlicet omnes prælati. Vos estis sal terræ, id est condimentum hominum in terra viventium, quia per discretionem et exemplarem conversationem vestram corda aliorum condiri seu dirigi debent, ut saporem habeant operum virtuosorum, et ut præserventur a putredine vitiorum, quemadmodum sal confert cibis saporem, et a putrefactione conservationem. Per sal ergo notatur discretio, quæ in omni opere necessaria est. Propter quod in Levitico dicitur : Quidquid obtuleris sacrificii, sale condies; in omni oblatione offeres sal. Unde ait Salvator : Habete in vobis sal. Et quia exempla superiorum maxime dirigunt et conservant animas subditorum, convenienter per sal designatur conversatio exemplaris.
paras.en: Although this sermon is said to have been addressed to the multitudes, it was nevertheless directed chiefly to the Apostles. For at the beginning of this chapter it was said: [[5:1|his disciples came unto him|Accesserunt ad eum discipuli ejus]], [[5:2|And opening his mouth he taught them|et aperiens os suum docebat eos]]. Luke also says: [[Luke 6:20|And he, lifting up his eyes on his disciples, said|Et ipse elevatis oculis in discipulis suis, dicebat]], etc. Addressing these same men, then, He now teaches what they ought to be, both they themselves and their successors, namely all prelates. [[5:13|You are the salt of the earth|Vos estis sal terræ]], that is, the seasoning of men living on the earth; for by your discretion and your exemplary manner of life the hearts of others ought to be seasoned or directed, so that they may have the savour of virtuous works and be preserved from the rottenness of vices, just as salt gives savour to food and preserves it from putrefaction. By salt, then, is signified discretion, which is necessary in every work. For this reason it is said in Leviticus: [[Lev 2:13|Whatsoever sacrifice thou offerest, thou shalt season it with salt|Quidquid obtuleris sacrificii, sale condies]]; [[Lev 2:13|In all thy oblations thou shalt offer salt|in omni oblatione tua offeres sal]]. Hence the Saviour says: [[Mark 9:49|Have salt in you|Habete in vobis sal]]. And because the examples of superiors most of all direct and preserve the souls of their subjects, an exemplary manner of life is fittingly designated by salt.

paras.t: Quod si sal evanuerit, hoc est, corruptum fuerit, et suum vigorem perdiderit, in quo salietur ? id est, quid illo condiri poterit? Nil utique. Tunc enim potius inficit cibum quam prosit. Ideo subditur : Ad nihilum valet ultra, nisi ut mittatur foras, hoc est, penitus effundatur, ne locum in domo inutiliter occupet, vel per errorem cibo immissum, ipsum corrumpat; et conculcetur ab hominibus in via ubi effusum est sal pergentibus. Per hoc insinuatur, quod prælatus indiscretus vel inexemplariter vivens, non condit, nec dirigit corda subditorum, nec potest eis prodesse, sed potius obest : idcirco prælatione indignus est, et ab ea avelli meretur, ac humiliari, atque subesse. Propterea Paulus admonet Timotheum, imo et omnem prælatum : Esto exemplum fidelium in verbo, in conversatione, in caritate : hoc enim faciens, et te ipsum salvum facies, et eos qui te audiunt.
paras.en: [[5:13|But if the salt lose its savour|Quod si sal evanuerit]], that is, if it be spoiled and lose its strength, [[5:13|wherewith shall it be salted?|in quo salietur?]] That is, what could be seasoned with it? Nothing at all. For then it rather infects the food than does it good. Therefore it is added: [[5:13|It is good for nothing anymore but to be cast out|ad nihilum valet ultra, nisi ut mittatur foras]], that is, to be poured out altogether, lest it take up room in the house to no purpose, or, put into food by mistake, spoil it; [[5:13|and to be trodden on by men|et conculcetur ab hominibus]] who walk along the road where the salt has been poured out. By this it is suggested that a prelate who is without discretion, or who does not live as an example, neither seasons nor directs the hearts of his subjects, nor can he do them good, but rather does them harm; and therefore he is unworthy of his prelacy, and deserves to be torn from it, humbled, and made a subject. For this reason Paul admonishes Timothy, and indeed every prelate: [[1 Tim 4:12|be thou an example of the faithful, in word, in conversation, in charity|exemplum esto fidelium in verbo, in conversatione, in caritate]]; [[1 Tim 4:16|For in doing this thou shalt both save thyself and them that hear thee|Hoc enim faciens, et teipsum salvum facies, et eos qui te audiunt]].

paras.t: Consequenter Christus comparat eos luci. Vos estis lux mundi, id est doctores hominum in mundo degentium, quoniam mentes aliorum illustrare debetis radio sapientiæ atque scientiæ, docendo eos quid credendum, quid sperandum, quid diligendum, quomodo discernere debeant inter bonum et malum, inter verum et falsum, inter pretiosum et vile. De talibus prælatis Dominus loquitur : Dabo vobis pastores juxta cor meum, et pascent vos scientia et doctrina. Ex his constat, quod pastor aliorum debeat esse actione præcipuus, et contemplatione sublimis, imo in utraque vita perfectus, ut valeat gregem ibi commissum instar cœlestis hierarchiæ purgare, illuminare, et perficere. Sed, heu ! multi jam aliorum curam suscipiunt, in quibus non est aqua sapientiæ salutaris, nec panis sanctæ conversationis. Qui si se ipsos diligenter attenderent, puto quod dicerent : Non sum medicus, et in domo mea non est panis ; nolite me constituere principem populi. De talibus loquitur Isaias quinquagesimo sexto capitulo : Speculatores cæci, canes muti non valentes latrare, videntes vana et dormientes.
paras.en: Next Christ compares them to light. [[5:14|You are the light of the world|Vos estis lux mundi]], that is, the teachers of men dwelling in the world; for you ought to enlighten the minds of others with the ray of wisdom and knowledge, teaching them what is to be believed, what hoped for, what loved, and how they ought to distinguish between good and evil, between true and false, between the precious and the vile. Of such prelates the Lord speaks: [[Jer 3:15|And I will give you pastors according to my own heart, and they shall feed you with knowledge and doctrine|Et dabo vobis pastores juxta cor meum, et pascent vos scientia et doctrina]]. From this it is clear that the shepherd of others ought to be outstanding in action and lofty in contemplation, indeed perfect in both lives, so that he may be able, after the likeness of the heavenly hierarchy, to purify, illuminate and perfect the flock committed to him [an allusion to the threefold hierarchical action described by Dionysius the Areopagite]. But alas! many now take up the care of others in whom there is neither the water of saving wisdom nor the bread of a holy manner of life. If they would look carefully at themselves, I think they would say: [[Is 3:7|I am no healer, and in my house there is no bread|Non sum medicus, et in domo mea non est panis]]; [[Is 3:7|make me not ruler of the people|nolite constituere me principem populi]]. Of such men Isaias speaks in the fifty-sixth chapter: Watchmen that are blind, [[Is 56:10|dumb dogs not able to bark, seeing vain things, sleeping|canes muti non valentes latrare, videntes vana, dormientes]].

paras.t: Sed quum de Joanne, quo major inter natos mulierum non surrexit, legatur, Non erat ille lux : quomodo Apostoli appellantur lux mundi? Et respondendum, quod Joannes non erat lux principalis et substantialis, sed ministerialis et participata. Denique triplex est lux, videlicet : lux illustrans, non illustrata, ut Deus : et sic Christus secundum divinam naturam lux erat, non Joannes. Lux illustrans et illustrata : tales præsertim fuerunt Joannes et sancti Apostoli, atque Prophetæ. Deinde gloriosus Dionysius, aliique doctores, dicuntur lux illustrata, non illustrans, sicut de pœnitentibus et conversis dicit Apostolus : Fuistis aliquando tenebræ, nunc autem lux in Domino.
paras.en: But since we read of John, than whom none greater has arisen among them that are born of women, [[John 1:8|He was not the light|Non erat ille lux]], how are the Apostles called the light of the world? It must be answered that John was not the principal and substantial light, but a ministering and participated one. For light is threefold. There is light that enlightens and is not enlightened, as God is: and in this sense Christ, according to His divine nature, was the light, and John was not. There is light that enlightens and is enlightened: such above all were John and the holy Apostles and the Prophets. Then the glorious Dionysius and the other doctors are called light that is enlightened [so the printed text; the sense seems to be that these, unlike the Apostles, receive the light without being its first ministers, like the penitents in the Apostle’s words], as the Apostle says of penitents and converts: [[Eph 5:8|For you were heretofore darkness, but now light in the Lord|Eratis enim aliquando tenebræ: nunc autem lux in Domino]].

paras.t: Quod autem Apostoli et prælati debeant sapientiam sibi communicatam aliis publice prædicare, eosque splendore virtutum ædificare, ostendit Salvator per duo quibus hi comparantur, videlicet per similitudinem civitatis altæ, et lucernæ accensæ. Non potest civitas abscondi supra montem posita, hoc est in loco sublimi constructa. Omnibus enim etiam a longinquo apparet. Sic vos aliorum pastores, seu Ecclesiæ prælati, qui estis fundati in Christo monte altissimo, de quo in Daniele asseritur, quod crevit in montem magnum, non debetis sapientiam vobis concessam abscondere, neque latere. Scriptum est enim : Sapientia abscondita et thesaurus invisus, quæ utilitas in utrisque ?
paras.en: That the Apostles and prelates ought to preach publicly to others the wisdom imparted to them, and to edify them by the splendour of their virtues, the Saviour shows by two things to which they are compared, namely by the likeness of a city set on high and of a lighted lamp.
